entries.a1f5c25b4b1d6777c354e229b1815016fda0f5b8: <div sID="gen9691" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="19" osisID="Job.19" sID="Job.19"/> <div eID="gen9691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9692" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9693" type="x-p"/> This chapter is Job's answer to Bildad's discourse in the foregoing chapter. Though his spirit was grieved and much heated, and Bildad was very peevish, yet he gave him leave to say all he designed to say, and did not break in upon him in the midst of his argument; but, when he had done, he gave him a fair answer, in which, I. He complains of unkind usage. And very unkindly he takes it. 1. That his comforters added to his affliction, <reference osisRef="Job.19.2-Job.19.7">ver. 2-7</reference>. 2. That his God was the author of his affliction, <reference osisRef="Job.19.8-Job.19.12">ver. 8-12</reference>. 3. That his relations and friends were strange to him, and shy of him, in his affliction, <reference osisRef="Job.19.20-Job.19.22">ver. 20-22</reference>. II. He comforts himself with the believing hopes of happiness in the other world, though he had so little comfort in this, making a very solemn confession of his faith, with a desire that it might be recorded as an evidence of his sincerity, <reference osisRef="Job.19.23-Job.19.27">ver. 23-27</reference>. III. He concludes with a caution to his friends not to persist in their hard censures of him, <reference osisRef="Job.19.28-Job.19.29">ver. 28, 29</reference>. If the remonstrance Job here makes of his grievances may serve sometimes to justify our complaints, yet his cheerful views of the future state, at the same time, may shame us Christians, and may serve to silence our complaints, or at least to balance them.
entries.ae581b1f3f4011a58bfb3d3ef25da3ed08cafff7: <div eID="gen9693" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9692" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Reply of Job to Bildad. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9694" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then Job answered and said, <hi type="super">2</hi> How long will ye vex my soul, and break me in pieces with words? <hi type="super">3</hi> These ten times have ye reproached me: ye are not ashamed <hi type="italic">that</hi> ye make yourselves strange to me. <hi type="super">4</hi> And be it indeed <hi type="italic">that</hi> I have erred, mine error remaineth with myself. 5 If indeed ye will magnify <hi type="italic">yourselves</hi> against me, and plead against me my reproach: <hi type="super">6</hi> Know now that God hath overthrown me, and hath compassed me with his net. <hi type="super">7</hi> Behold, I cry out of wrong, but I am not heard: I cry aloud, but <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no judgment. <div eID="gen9694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9695" type="x-p"/> Job's friends had passed a very severe censure upon him as a wicked man because he was so grievously afflicted; now here he tells them how ill he took it to be so censured. Bildad had twice begun with a <hi type="italic">How long</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.8.2">ch. viii. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.18.2">xviii. 2</reference>), and therefore Job, being now to answer him particularly, begins with a <hi type="italic">How long</hi> too, <reference osisRef="Job.19.2">v. 2</reference>. What is not liked is commonly thought long; but Job had more reason to think those long who assaulted him than they had to think him long who only vindicated himself. Better cause may be shown for defending ourselves, if we have right on our side, than for offending our brethren, though we have right on our side. Now observe here, <div eID="gen9695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9696" type="x-p"/> I. How he describes their unkindness to him and what account he gives of it. 1. They <hi type="italic">vexed his soul,</hi> and that is more grievous than the vexation of the bones, <reference osisRef="Ps.6.2-Ps.6.3">Ps. vi. 2, 3</reference>. They were his friends; they came to comfort him, pretended to counsel him for the best; but with a great deal of gravity, and affectation of wisdom and piety, they set themselves to rob him of the only comfort he had now left him in a good God, a good conscience, and a good name; and this vexed him to his heart. 2. They <hi type="italic">broke him in pieces with words,</hi> and those were surely hard and very cruel words that would break a man to pieces: they grieved him, and so broke him; and therefore there will be a reckoning hereafter for all the hard speeches spoken against Christ and his people, <reference osisRef="Jude.1.15">Jude 15</reference>. 3. They <hi type="italic">reproached him,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.19.3">v. 3</reference>), gave him a bad character and laid to his charge things that he knew not. To an ingenuous mind reproach is a cutting thing. 4. They <hi type="italic">made themselves strange to him,</hi> were shy of him now that he was in his troubles, and seemed as if they did not know him (<reference osisRef="Job.2.12">ch. ii. 12</reference>), were not free with him as they used to be when he was in his prosperity. Those are governed by the spirit of the world, and not by any principles of true honour or love, who make themselves strange to their friends, or God's friends, when they are in trouble. <hi type="italic">A friend loves at all times.</hi> 5. They not only estranged themselves from him, but <hi type="italic">magnified themselves against him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.19.5">v. 5</reference>), not only looked shy of him, but looked big upon him, and insulted over him, magnifying themselves to depress him. It is a mean thing, it is a base thing, thus to trample upon those that are down. 6. <hi type="italic">They pleaded against him his reproach,</hi> that is, they made use of his affliction as an argument against him to prove him a wicked man. They should have pleaded for him his integrity, and helped him to take the comfort of that under his affliction, and so have pleaded that against his reproach (as St. Paul, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.12">2 Cor. i. 12</reference>); but, instead of that, they pleaded his reproach against his integrity, which was not only unkind, but very unjust; for where shall we find an honest man if reproach may be admitted for a plea against him? <div eID="gen9696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9697" type="x-p"/> II. How he aggravates their unkindness. 1. They had thus abused him often (<reference osisRef="Job.19.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">These ten times you have reproached me,</hi> that is, very often, as <reference osisRef="Gen.31.7">Gen. xxxi. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.14.22">Num. xiv. 22</reference>. Five times they had spoken, and every speech was a double reproach. He spoke as if he had kept a particular account of their reproaches, and could tell just how many they were. It is but a peevish and unfriendly thing to do so, and looks like a design of retaliation and revenge. We better befriend our own peace by forgetting injuries and unkindnesses than by remembering them and scoring them up. 2. They continued still to abuse him, and seemed resolved to persist in it: "How long will you do it?" <reference osisRef="Job.19.2">v. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.19.5">5</reference>. "I see you will magnify yourselves against me, notwithstanding all I have said in my own justification." Those that speak too much seldom think they have said enough; and, when the mouth is opened in passion, the ear is shut to reason. 3. They were not ashamed of what they did, <reference osisRef="Job.19.3">v. 3</reference>. They had reason to be ashamed of their hard-heartedness, so ill becoming men, of their uncharitableness, so ill becoming good men, and of their deceitfulness, so ill becoming friends: but were they ashamed? No, though they were told of it again and again, yet they could not blush. <div eID="gen9697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9698" type="x-p"/> III. How he answers their harsh censures, by showing them that what they condemned was capable of excuse, which they ought to have considered. 1. The errors of his judgment were excusable (<reference osisRef="Job.19.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Be it indeed that I have erred,</hi> that I am in the wrong through ignorance or mistake," which may well be supposed concerning men, concerning good men. <hi type="italic">Humanum est errare</hi>—<hi type="italic">Error cleaves to humanity;</hi> and we must be willing to suppose it concerning ourselves. It is folly to think ourselves infallible. "But be it so," said Job, "<hi type="italic">my error remaineth with myself,</hi>" that is, "I speak according to the best of my judgment, with all sincerity, and not from a spirit of contradiction." Or, "If I be in an error, I keep it to myself, and do not impose it upon others as you do. I only prove myself and my own work by it. I meddle not with other people, either to teach them or to judge them." Men's errors are the more excusable if they keep them to themselves, and do not disturb others with them. <hi type="italic">Hast thou faith? Have it to thyself.</hi> Some give this sense of these words: "If I be in an error, it is I that must smart for it; and therefore you need not concern yourselves: nay, it is I that do smart, and smart severely, for it; and therefore you need not add to my misery by your reproaches." 2. The breakings out of his passion, though not justifiable, yet were excusable, considering the vastness of his grief and the extremity of his misery. "If you will go on to cavil at every complaining word I speak, will make the worst of it and improve it against me, yet take the cause of the complaint along with you, and weigh that, before you pass a judgment upon the complaint, and turn it to my reproach: <hi type="italic">Know then that God has overthrown me,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Job.19.6">v. 6</reference>. Three things he would have them consider:—(1.) That his trouble was very great. He was overthrown, and could not help himself, enclosed as in a net, and could not get out. (2.) That God was the author of it, and that, in it, he fought against him: "It was his hand that overthrew me; it is in his net that I am enclosed; and therefore you need not appear against me thus. I have enough to do to grapple with God's displeasure; let me not have yours also. Let God's controversy with me be ended before you begin yours." It is barbarous to <hi type="italic">persecute him whom God hath smitten and to talk to the grief of one whom he hath wounded,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.69.26">Ps. lxix. 26</reference>. (3.) That he could not obtain any hope of the redress of his grievances, <reference osisRef="Job.19.7">v. 7</reference>. He complained of his pain, but got no ease—begged to know the cause of his affliction, but could not discover it—appealed to God's tribunal for the clearing of his innocency, but could not obtain a hearing, much less a judgment, upon his appeal: <hi type="italic">I cry out of wrong, but I am not heard.</hi> God, for a time, may seem to turn away his ear from his people, to be angry at their prayers and overlook their appeals to him, and they must be excused if, in that case, they complain bitterly. Woe unto us if God be against us!
entries.5ded5e30077943e99e5a3b0bcdab59c7df7c416a: <div eID="gen9698" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Job Complains of God's Displeasure; Job Complains of His Friends. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9699" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> He hath fenced up my way that I cannot pass, and he hath set darkness in my paths. <hi type="super">9</hi> He hath stripped me of my glory, and taken the crown <hi type="italic">from</hi> my head. <hi type="super">10</hi> He hath destroyed me on every side, and I am gone: and mine hope hath he removed like a tree. <hi type="super">11</hi> He hath also kindled his wrath against me, and he counteth me unto him as <hi type="italic">one of</hi> his enemies. <hi type="super">12</hi> His troops come together, and raise up their way against me, and encamp round about my tabernacle. <hi type="super">13</hi> He hath put my brethren far from me, and mine acquaintance are verily estranged from me. <hi type="super">14</hi> My kinsfolk have failed, and my familiar friends have forgotten me. <hi type="super">15</hi> They that dwell in mine house, and my maids, count me for a stranger: I am an alien in their sight. <hi type="super">16</hi> I called my servant, and he gave <hi type="italic">me</hi> no answer; I intreated him with my mouth. <hi type="super">17</hi> My breath is strange to my wife, though I intreated for the children's <hi type="italic">sake</hi> of mine own body. <hi type="super">18</hi> Yea, young children despised me; I arose, and they spake against me. <hi type="super">19</hi> All my inward friends abhorred me: and they whom I loved are turned against me. <hi type="super">20</hi> My bone cleaveth to my skin and to my flesh, and I am escaped with the skin of my teeth. <hi type="super">21</hi> Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O ye my friends; for the hand of God hath touched me. <hi type="super">22</hi> Why do ye persecute me as God, and are not satisfied with my flesh? <div eID="gen9699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9700" type="x-p"/> Bildad had very disingenuously perverted Job's complaints by making them the description of the miserable condition of a wicked man; and yet he repeats them here, to move their pity, and to work upon their good nature, if they had any left in them. <div eID="gen9700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9701" type="x-p"/> I. He complains of the tokens of God's displeasure which he was under, and which infused the wormwood and gall into the affliction and misery. How doleful are the accents of his complaints! "<hi type="italic">He hath kindled his wrath against me,</hi> which flames and terrifies me, which burns and pains me," <reference osisRef="Job.19.11">v. 11</reference>. What is the fire of hell but the wrath of God? Seared consciences will feel it hereafter, but do not fear it now. Enlightened consciences fear it now, but shall not feel it hereafter. Job's present apprehension was that <hi type="italic">God counted him as one of his enemies;</hi> and yet, at the same time, God loved him, and gloried in him, as his faithful friend. It is a gross mistake, but a very common one, to think that whom God afflicts he treats as his enemies; whereas, on the contrary, <hi type="italic">as many as he loves he rebukes and chastens;</hi> it is the discipline of his sons. Which way soever Job looked he thought he saw the tokens of God's displeasure against him. 1. Did he look back upon his former prosperity? He saw God's hand putting an end to that (<reference osisRef="Job.19.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">He has stripped me of my glory,</hi> my wealth, honour, power, and all the opportunity I had of doing good. My children were my glory, but I have lost them; and whatever was a crown to my head he has taken it from me, and has laid all my honour in the dust." See the vanity of worldly glory: it is what we may be soon stripped of; and, whatever strips us, we must see and own God's hand in it and comply with his design. 2. Did he look down upon his present troubles? He saw God giving them their commission, and their orders to attack him. They are <hi type="italic">his troops,</hi> that act by his direction, which <hi type="italic">encamp against me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.19.12">v. 12</reference>. It did not so much trouble him that his miseries came upon him in troops as that they were <hi type="italic">God's</hi> troops, in whom it seemed as if God fought against him and intended his destruction. God's troops <hi type="italic">encamped around his tabernacle,</hi> as soldiers lay siege to a strong city, cutting off all provisions from being brought into it and battering it continually; thus was Job's tabernacle besieged. Time was when God's hosts encamped round him for safety: <hi type="italic">Hast thou not made a hedge about him?</hi> Now, on the contrary, they surrounded him, to his terror, and <hi type="italic">destroyed him on every side,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.19.10">v. 10</reference>. 3. Did he look forward for deliverance? He saw the hand of God cutting off all hopes of that (<reference osisRef="Job.19.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">He hath fenced up my way, that I cannot pass.</hi> I have now no way left to help myself, either to extricate myself out of my troubles or to ease myself under them. Would I make any motion, take any steps towards deliverance? I find <hi type="italic">my way hedged up;</hi> I cannot do what I would; nay, if I would please myself with the prospect of a deliverance hereafter, I cannot do it; it is not only out of my reach, but out of my sight: God <hi type="italic">hath set darkness in my paths,</hi> and there is none to tell me how long," <reference osisRef="Ps.74.9">Ps. lxxiv. 9</reference>. He concludes (<reference osisRef="Job.19.10">v. 10</reference>), "I am gone, quite lost and undone for this world; <hi type="italic">my hope hath he removed like a tree</hi> cut down, or plucked up by the roots, which will never grow again." Hope in this life is a perishing thing, but the hope of good men, when it is cut off from this world, is but removed like a tree, transplanted from this nursery to the garden of the Lord. We shall have no reason to complain if God thus remove our hopes from the sand to the rock, from things temporal to things eternal. <div eID="gen9701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9702" type="x-p"/> II. He complains of the unkindness of his relations and of all his old acquaintance. In this also he owns the hand of God (<reference osisRef="Job.19.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">He has put my brethren far from me,</hi> that is, "He has laid those afflictions upon me which frighten them from me, and make them stand aloof from my sores." As it was their sin God was not the author of it; it is Satan that alienates men's minds from their brethren in affliction. But, as it was Job's trouble, God ordered it for the completing of his trial. As we must eye the hand of God in all the injuries we receive from our enemies ("the Lord has bidden Shimei curse David"), so also in all the slights and unkindnesses we receive from our friends, which will help us to bear them the more patiently. Every creature is that to us (kind or unkind, comfortable or uncomfortable) which God makes it to be. Yet this does not excuse Job's relations and friends from the guilt of horrid ingratitude and injustice to him, which he had reason to complain of; few could have borne it so well as he did. He takes notice of the unkindness, 1. Of his kindred and acquaintance, his neighbours, and such as he had formerly been familiar with, who were bound by all the laws of friendship and civility to concern themselves for him, to visit him, to enquire after him, and to be ready to do him all the good offices that lay in their power; yet these were <hi type="italic">estranged from him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.19.13">v. 13</reference>. They took no more care about him than if he had been a stranger whom they never knew. His kinsfolk, who claimed relation to him when he was in prosperity, now failed him; they came short of their former professions of friendship to him and his present expectations of kindness from them. Even his familiar friends, whom he was mindful of, had now forgotten him, had forgotten both his former friendliness to them and his present miseries: they had heard of his troubles, and designed him a visit; but truly they forgot it, so little affected were they with it. Nay, his inward friends, the men of his secret, whom he was most intimate with and laid in his bosom, not only forgot him, but abhorred him, kept as far off from him as they could, because he was poor and could not entertain them as he used to do, and because he was sore and a loathsome spectacle. Those whom he loved, and who therefore were worse than publicans if they did not love him now that he was in distress, not only turned from him, but were turned against him, and did all they could to make him odious, so to justify themselves in being so strange to him, <reference osisRef="Job.19.19">v. 19</reference>. So uncertain is the friendship of men; but, if God be our friend, he will not fail us in a time of need. But let none that pretend either to humanity or Christianity ever use their friends as Job's friends used him: adversity is the proof of friendship. 2. Of his domestics and family relations. Sometimes indeed we find that, beyond our expectation, there is a friend that sticks closer than a brother; but the master of a family ordinarily expects to be attended on and taken care of by those of his family, even when, through weakness of body or mind, he has become despicable to others. But poor Job was misused by his own family, and some of his worst foes were those of his own house. He mentions not his children; they were all dead, and we may suppose that the unkindness of his surviving relations made him lament the death of his children so much the more: "If they had been alive," would he think, "I should have had comfort in them." As for those that were now about him, (1.) His own servants slighted him. His maids did not attend him in his illness, but <hi type="italic">counted him for a stranger and an alien,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.19.15">v. 15</reference>. His other servants never heeded him; if he called to them they would not come at his call, but pretended that they did not hear him. If he asked them a question, they would not vouchsafe to <hi type="italic">give him an answer,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.19.16">v. 16</reference>. Job had been a good master to them, and did not <hi type="italic">despise their cause when they pleaded with him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.31.13">ch. xxxi. 13</reference>), and yet they were rude to him now, and despised his cause when he pleaded with them. We must not think it strange if we receive evil at the hand of those from whom we have deserved well. Though he was now sickly, yet he was not cross with his servants, and imperious, as is too common, but he entreated his servants with his mouth, when he had authority to command; and yet they would not be civil to him, neither kind nor just. Note, Those that are sick and in sorrow are apt to take things ill, and be jealous of a slight, and to lay to heart the least unkindness done to them: when Job was in affliction even his servants' neglect of him troubled him. (2.) But, one would think, when all forsook him, the wife of his bosom should have been tender of him: no, because he would not curse God and die, as she persuaded him, his breath was strange to her too; she did not care for coming near him, nor took any notice of what he said, <reference osisRef="Job.19.17">v. 17</reference>. Though he spoke to her, not with the authority, but with the tenderness of a husband, did not command, but entreated her by that conjugal love which their children were the pledges of, yet she regarded him not. Some read it, "Though I lamented, or bemoaned myself, for the children," that is, "for the death of the children of my own body," an affliction in which she was equally concerned with him. Now, it appeared, the devil spared her to him, not only to be his tempter, but to be his tormentor. By what she said to him at first, <hi type="italic">Curse God and die,</hi> it appeared that she had little religion in her; and what can one expect that is kind and good from those that have not the fear of God before their eyes and are not governed by conscience? (3.) Even the little children who were born in his house, the children of his own servants, who were his servants by birth, despised him, and spoke against him (<reference osisRef="Job.19.18">v. 18</reference>); though he arose in civility to speak friendly to them, or with authority to check them, they let him know that they neither feared him nor loved him. <div eID="gen9702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9703" type="x-p"/> III. He complains of the decay of his body; all the beauty and strength of that were gone. When those about him slighted him, if he had been in health, and at ease, he might have enjoyed himself. But he could take as little pleasure in himself as others took in him (<reference osisRef="Job.19.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">My bone cleaves now to my skin,</hi> as formerly it did to my flesh; it was this that filled <hi type="italic">him with wrinkles</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.16.8">ch. xvi. 8</reference>); he was a perfect skeleton, nothing but skin and bones. Nay, his skin too was almost gone, little remained unbroken but the <hi type="italic">skin of his teeth,</hi> his gums and perhaps his lips; all the rest was fetched off by his sore boils. See what little reason we have to indulge the body, which, after all our care, may be thus consumed by the diseases which it has in itself the seeds of. <div eID="gen9703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9704" type="x-p"/> IV. Upon all these accounts he recommends himself to the compassion of his friends, and justly blames their harshness with him. From this representation of his deplorable case, it was easy to infer, 1. That they ought to pity him, <reference osisRef="Job.19.21">v. 21</reference>. This he begs in the most moving melting language that could be, enough (one would think) to break a heart of stone: "<hi type="italic">Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O you my friends!</hi> if you will do nothing else for me, be sorry for me, and show some concern for me; <hi type="italic">have pity upon me, for the hand of God hath touched me.</hi> My case is sad indeed, for I have fallen into the hands of the living God, my spirit is touched with the sense of his wrath, a calamity of all other the most piteous." Note, It becomes friends to pity one another when they are in trouble, and not to shut up the bowels of compassion. 2. That, however, they ought not to persecute him; if they would not ease his affliction by their pity, yet they must not be so barbarous as to add to it by their censures and reproaches (<reference osisRef="Job.19.22">v. 22</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Why do you persecute me as God?</hi> Surely his rebukes are enough for one man to bear; you need not add your wormwood and gall to the cup of affliction he puts into my hand, it is bitter enough without that: God has a sovereign power over me, and may do what he pleases with me; but do you think that you may do so too?" No, we must aim to be like the Most Holy and the Most Merciful, but not like the Most High and Most Mighty. God gives not account of any of his matters, but we must give account of ours. If they did delight in his calamity, let them be satisfied with his flesh, which was wasted and gone, but let them not, as if that were too little, wound his spirit, and ruin his good name. Great tenderness is due to those that are in affliction, especially to those that are troubled in mind.
entries.2a1a2fd5e3ea5af512825e3496250a190e040e51: <div eID="gen9704" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Job's Confession of Faith; Happiness of the Redeemed. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9705" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> Oh that my words were now written! oh that they were printed in a book! <hi type="super">24</hi> That they were graven with an iron pen and lead in the rock for ever! <hi type="super">25</hi> For I know <hi type="italic">that</hi> my redeemer liveth, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> he shall stand at the latter <hi type="italic">day</hi> upon the earth: <hi type="super">26</hi> And <hi type="italic">though</hi> after my skin <hi type="italic">worms</hi> destroy this <hi type="italic">body,</hi> yet in my flesh shall I see God: <hi type="super">27</hi> Whom I shall see for myself, and mine eyes shall behold, and not another; <hi type="italic">though</hi> my reins be consumed within me. <hi type="super">28</hi> But ye should say, Why persecute we him, seeing the root of the matter is found in me? <hi type="super">29</hi> Be ye afraid of the sword: for wrath <hi type="italic">bringeth</hi> the punishments of the sword, that ye may know <hi type="italic">there is</hi> a judgment. <div eID="gen9705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9706" type="x-p"/> In all the conferences between Job and his friends we do not find any more weighty and considerable lines than these; would one have expected it? Here is much both of Christ and heaven in these verses: and he that said such things as these <hi type="italic">declared plainly that he sought the better country, that is, the heavenly;</hi> as the patriarchs of that age did, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.14">Heb. xi. 14</reference>. We have here Job's creed, or confession of faith. His belief in God the Father Almighty, the Maker of heaven and earth, and the principles of natural religion, he had often professed: but here we find him no stranger to revealed religion; though the revelation of the promised Seed, and the promised inheritance, was then discerned only like the dawning of the day, yet Job was taught of God to believe in a living Redeemer, and to <hi type="italic">look for the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come,</hi> for of these, doubtless, he must be understood to speak. These were the things he comforted himself with the expectation of, and not a deliverance from his trouble or a revival of his happiness in this world, as some would understand him; for besides that the expressions he here uses, of the Redeemer's <hi type="italic">standing at the latter day upon the earth,</hi> of his seeing God, and <hi type="italic">seeing him for himself,</hi> are wretchedly forced if they be understood of any temporal deliverance, it is very plain that he had no expectation at all of his return to a prosperous condition in this world. He had just now said that <hi type="italic">his way was fenced up,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.19.8">v. 8</reference>) and his <hi type="italic">hope removed like a tree,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.19.10">v. 10</reference>. Nay, and after this he expressed his despair of any comfort in this life, <reference osisRef="Job.23.8-Job.23.9">ch. xxiii. 8, 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.30.23">xxx. 23</reference>. So that we must necessarily understand him of the redemption of his soul from the power of the grave, and his reception to glory, which is spoken of, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.15">Ps. xlix. 15</reference>. We have reason to think that Job was just now under an extraordinary impulse of the blessed Spirit, which raised him above himself, gave him light, and gave him utterance, even to his own surprise. And some observe that, after this, we do not find Job's discourses such passionate, peevish, unbecoming, complaints of God and his providence as we have before met with: this hope quieted his spirit, stilled the storm and, having here cast anchor within the veil, his mind was kept steady from this time forward. Let us observe, <div eID="gen9706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9707" type="x-p"/> I. To what intent Job makes this confession of his faith here. Never did any thing come in more pertinently, or to better purpose. 1. Job was now accused, and this was his appeal. His friends reproached him as a hypocrite and contemned him as a wicked man; but he appeals to his creed, to his faith, to his hope, and to his own conscience, which not only acquitted him from reigning sin, but comforted him with the expectation of a blessed resurrection. <hi type="italic">These are not the words of him that has a devil.</hi> He appeals to the coming of the Redeemer, from this wrangle at the bar to the judgment of the bench, even to him to whom all judgment is committed, who he knew would right him. The consideration of God's day coming will make it a <hi type="italic">very small thing with us to be judged of man's judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.3-1Cor.4.4">1 Cor. iv. 3, 4</reference>. How easily may we bear the unjust calumnies and reproaches of men while we expect the glorious appearance of our Redeemer, and his redeemed, at the last day, and that there will then be a resurrection of names, as well as bodies! 2. Job was now afflicted, and this was his cordial; when he was pressed above measure this kept him from fainting—he believed that he should <hi type="italic">see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living;</hi> not in this world, for that is the land of the dying. <div eID="gen9707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9708" type="x-p"/> II. With what a solemn preface he introduces it, <reference osisRef="Job.19.23-Job.19.24">v. 23, 24</reference>. He breaks off his complaints abruptly, to triumph his comforts, which he does, not only for his own satisfaction, but for the edification of others. Those now about him, he feared, would little regard what he said, and so it proved, He therefore wished it might be recorded for the generations to come. <hi type="italic">O that my words were now written,</hi> the words I am now about to say! As if he had said, "I own I have spoken many unadvised words, which I could wish might be forgotten, for they will neither do me credit nor do others good. But I am now going to speak deliberately, and that which I desire may be published to all the world and preserved for the generations to come, <hi type="italic">in perpetuam rei memoriam</hi>—<hi type="italic">for an abiding memorial,</hi> and therefore that it may be written plainly and <hi type="italic">printed,</hi> or drawn out in large and legible characters, so that he that runs may read it; and that it may not be left in loose papers, but put into <hi type="italic">a book;</hi> or, if that should perish, that it may be <hi type="italic">engraven</hi> like an inscription upon a monument, <hi type="italic">with an iron pen in lead, or in the stone;</hi> let the engraver use all his art to make it a durable appeal to posterity." That which Job here somewhat passionately wished for God graciously granted him. His words are written; they are printed in God's book; so that, wherever that book is read, there shall this be told for a memorial concerning Job. He believed, therefore he spoke. <div eID="gen9708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9709" type="x-p"/> III. What his confession itself is; what are the words which he would have to be written; we here have them written, <reference osisRef="Job.19.25-Job.19.27">v. 25-27</reference>. Let us observe them. <div eID="gen9709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9710" type="x-p"/> 1. He believes the glory of the Redeemer and his own interest in him (<reference osisRef="Job.19.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">I know that my Redeemer liveth,</hi> that he is in being and is my life, <hi type="italic">and that he shall stand at last,</hi> or stand the last, or at the latter day, <hi type="italic">upon</hi> (or above) <hi type="italic">the earth.</hi> He shall be raised up, or, He shall be, at the latter day, (that is, in the fulness of time: the gospel day is called <hi type="italic">the last time</hi> because that is the last dispensation) upon the earth: so it points at his incarnation; or, He shall be lifted up from the earth (so it points at his crucifixion), or raised up out of the earth (so it is applicable to his resurrection), or, as we commonly understand it, At the end of time he shall appear over the earth, for <hi type="italic">he shall come in the clouds, and every eye shall see him,</hi> so close shall he come to this earth. He shall stand <hi type="italic">upon the dust</hi> (so the word is), upon all his enemies, which shall be put a dust under his feet; and he shall tread upon them and triumph over them. Observe here, (1.) That there is a Redeemer provided for fallen man, and Jesus Christ is that Redeemer. The word is <hi type="italic">Go&#235;l</hi> which is used for the next of kin, to whom, by the law of Moses, the right of redeeming a mortgaged estate did belong, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.25">Lev. xxv. 25</reference>. Our heavenly inheritance was mortgaged by sin; we are ourselves utterly unable to redeem it; Christ is near of kin to us, the next kinsman that is able to redeem; he has paid our debt, satisfied God's justice for sin, and so has taken off the mortgage and made a new settlement of the inheritance. Our persons also want a Redeemer; we are sold for sin, and sold under sin; our Lord Jesus has wrought out a redemption for us, and proclaims redemption for us, and proclaims redemption to us, and so he is truly the Redeemer. (2.) He is a living Redeemer. As we are made by a living God, so we are saved by a living Redeemer, who is both almighty and eternal, and is therefore able to save to the uttermost. <hi type="italic">Of him it is witnessed that he liveth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.7.8">Heb. vii. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.18">Rev. i. 18</reference>. We are dying, but he liveth, and hath assured us that <hi type="italic">because he lives we shall live also,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.14.19">John xiv. 19</reference>. (3.) There are those that through grace have an interest in this Redeemer, and can, upon good grounds, call him theirs. When Job had lost all his wealth and all his friends, yet he was not separated from Christ, nor cut off from his relation to him: "Still he is my Redeemer." That next kinsman adhered to him when all his other kindred forsook him, and he had the comfort of it. (4.) Our interest in the Redeemer is a thing that may be known; and, where it is known, it may be triumphed in, as sufficient to balance all our griefs: <hi type="italic">I know</hi> (observe with what an air of assurance he speaks it, as one confident of this very thing), <hi type="italic">I know that my Redeemer lives.</hi> His friends have often charged him with ignorance or vain knowledge; but he knows enough, and knows to good purpose, who knows Christ to be his Redeemer. (5.) There will be a latter day, a last day, a day when <hi type="italic">time shall be no more,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.10.6">Rev. x. 6</reference>. That is a day we are concerned to think of every day. (6.) Our Redeemer will at that day stand upon the earth, or over the earth, to summon the dead out of their graves, and determine them to an unchangeable state; for to him all judgment is committed. He shall stand, at the last, on the dust to which this earth will be reduced by the conflagration. <div eID="gen9710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9711" type="x-p"/> 2. He believes the happiness of the redeemed, and his own title to that happiness, that, at Christ's second coming, believers shall be raised up in glory and so made perfectly blessed in the vision and fruition of God; and this he believes with application to himself. (1.) He counts upon the corrupting of his body in the grave, and speaks of it with a holy carelessness and unconcernedness: <hi type="italic">Though, after my skin</hi> (which is already wasted and gone, none of it remaining but <hi type="italic">the skin of my teeth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.19.20">v. 20</reference>) <hi type="italic">they destroy</hi> (those that are appointed to destroy it, the grave and the worms in it of which he had spoken, <reference osisRef="Job.17.14">ch. xvii. 14</reference>) <hi type="italic">this body.</hi> The word <hi type="italic">body</hi> is added: "Though they destroy this, this skeleton, this shadow (<reference osisRef="Job.17.7">ch. xvii. 7</reference>), this that I lay my hand upon," or (pointing perhaps to his weak and withered limbs) "this that you see, call it what you will; I expect that shortly it will be a feast for the worms." Christ's body saw not corruption, but ours must. And Job mentions this, that the glory of the resurrection he believed and hoped for might shine the more brightly. Note, It is good for us often to think, not only of the approaching death of our bodies, but of their destruction and dissolution in the grave; yet let not that discourage our hope of their resurrection, for the same power that made man's body at first, out of common dust, can raise it out of its own dust. This body which we now take such care about, and make such provision for, will in a little time be destroyed. Even <hi type="italic">my reins</hi> (says Job) <hi type="italic">shall be consumed within me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.19.27">v. 27</reference>); the innermost part of the body, which perhaps putrefies first. (2.) He comforts himself with the hopes of happiness on the other side death and the grave: <hi type="italic">After I shall awake</hi> (so the margin reads it), <hi type="italic">though this body be destroyed, yet out of my flesh shall I see God.</hi> [1.] Soul and body shall come together again. That body which must be destroyed in the grave shall be raised again, a glorious body: <hi type="italic">Yet in my flesh I shall see God.</hi> The separate soul has eyes wherewith to see God, eyes of the mind; but Job speaks of seeing him with eyes of flesh, <hi type="italic">in my flesh, with my eyes;</hi> the same body that died shall rise again, a true body, but a glorified body, fit for the employments and entertainments of that world, and therefore a <hi type="italic">spiritual body,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.44">1 Cor. xv. 44</reference>. Let us <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> glorify God with our bodies because there is such a glory designed for them. [2.] Job and God shall come together again: <hi type="italic">In my flesh shall I see God,</hi> that is, the glorified Redeemer, who is God. <hi type="italic">I shall see God in my flesh</hi> (so some read it), the Son of God clothed with a body which will be visible even to eyes of flesh. Though the body, in the grave, seem despicable and miserable, yet it shall be dignified and made happy in the vision of God. Job now complained that he could not get a sight of God (<reference osisRef="Job.23.8-Job.23.9">ch. xxiii. 8, 9</reference>), but hoped to see him shortly, never more to lose the sight of him, and that sight of him will be the more welcome after the present darkness and distance. Note, It is the blessedness of the blessed that they shall see God, shall see him as he is, see him face to face, and no longer through a glass darkly. See with what pleasure holy Job enlarges upon this (<reference osisRef="Job.19.27">v. 27</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Whom I shall see for myself,</hi>" that is, "see and enjoy, see to my own unspeakable comfort and satisfaction. I shall see him as mine, as mine with an appropriating sight," <reference osisRef="Rev.21.3">Rev. xxi. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">God himself shall be with them and be their God;</hi> they shall be <hi type="italic">like him, for they shall see him as he is,</hi> that is seeing for themselves, <reference osisRef="1John.3.2">1 John iii. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">My eyes shall behold him, and not another. First,</hi> "He, and not another for him, shall be seen, not a type or figure of him, but he himself." Glorified saints are perfectly sure that they are not imposed upon; it is no <hi type="italic">deceptio visus—illusion of the senses. Secondly,</hi> "I, and not another for me, shall see him. Though my flesh and body be consumed, yet I shall not need a proxy; I shall see him with my own eyes." This was what Job hoped for, and what he earnestly desired, which, some think, is the meaning of the last clause: <hi type="italic">My reins are spent in my bosom,</hi> that is, "all my desires are summed up and concluded in this; this will crown and complete them all; let me have this, and I shall have nothing more to desire; it is enough; it is all." With this the prayers of David, the son of Jesse, are ended. <div eID="gen9711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9712" type="x-p"/> IV. The application of this to his friends. His creed spoke comfort to himself, but warning and terror to those that set themselves against him. <div eID="gen9712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9713" type="x-p"/> 1. It was a word of caution to them not to proceed and persist in their unkind usage of him, <reference osisRef="Job.19.28">v. 28</reference>. He had reproved them for what they had said, and now tells them what they should say for the reducing of themselves and one another to a better temper. "<hi type="italic">Why persecute we him</hi> thus? Why do we grieve him and vex him, by censuring and condemning him, <hi type="italic">seeing the root of the matter,</hi> or the root of the word, <hi type="italic">is found in him?</hi>" Let this direct us, (1.) In our care concerning ourselves. We are all concerned to see to it that the root of the matter be found in us. A living, quickening, commanding, principle of grace in the heart, is the root of the matter, as necessary to our religion as the root to the tree, to which it owes both its fixedness and its fruitfulness. Love to God and our brethren, faith in Christ, hatred of sin—these are the root of the matter; other things are but leaves in comparison with these. Serious godliness is the one thing needful. (2.) In our conduct towards our brethren. We are to believe that many have the root of the matter in them who are not in every thing of our mind—who have their follies, and weaknesses, and mistakes—and to conclude that it is at our peril if we persecute any such. Woe be to him that offends one of those little ones! God will resent and revenge it. Job and his friends differed in some notions concerning the methods of Providence, but they agreed in the root of the matter, the belief of another world, and therefore should not persecute one another for these differences. <div eID="gen9713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9714" type="x-p"/> 2. It was a word of terror to them. Christ's second coming will be very dreadful to those that are found <hi type="italic">smiting their fellow servants</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.49">Matt. xxiv. 49</reference>), and therefore (<reference osisRef="Job.19.29">v. 29</reference>), "<hi type="italic">Be you afraid of the sword,</hi> the flaming sword of God's justice, which turns every way; fear, lest you make yourselves obnoxious to it." Good men need to be frightened from sin by the terrors of the Almighty, particularly from the sin of rashly judging their brethren, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.1">Matt. vii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.3.1">Jam. iii. 1</reference>. Those that are peevish and passionate with their brethren, censorious of them and malicious towards them, should know, not only that their wrath, whatever it pretends, works not the righteousness of God, but that, (1.) They may expect to smart for it in this world: <hi type="italic">It brings the punishments of the sword.</hi> Wrath leads to such crimes as expose men to the sword of the magistrate. God himself often takes vengeance for it, and those that showed no mercy shall find no mercy. (2.) If they repent not, that will be an earnest of worse. By these you may know there is a judgment, not only a present government, but a future judgment, in which hard speeches must be accounted for.  <chapter eID="Job.19"/> <div eID="gen9714" type="x-p"/>

Job's Reply to Bildad.</title> <div sID="gen7087" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4845"/><hi type="bold">2. How long, &c.--</hi>retorting Bildad's words (<reference osisRef="Job.18.2">Job 18:2</reference>). Admitting the punishment to be deserved, is it kind thus ever to be harping on this to the sufferer? And yet even this they have not yet proved. <div eID="gen7087" type="x-p"/>

These--</hi>prefixed emphatically to numbers (<reference osisRef="Gen.27.36">Ge 27:36</reference>).<div eID="gen7088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7089" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ten--</hi>that is, often (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.7">Ge 31:7</reference>).<div eID="gen7089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7090" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make yourselves strange--</hi>rather, "stun me" [Gesenius]. (See Margin for a different meaning [that is, "harden yourselves against me"]).<div eID="gen7090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7091" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4.erred--</hi>The Hebrew expresses unconscious error. Job was unconscious of wilful sin.<div eID="gen7091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7092" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remaineth--</hi>literally, "passeth the night." An image from harboring an unpleasant guest for the night. I bear the consequences. <div eID="gen7092" type="x-p"/>
entries.94ac568bb967e65b1549d1fdaab67028ba4a604c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4847"/><div sID="gen7093" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4847"/><hi type="bold">5. magnify, &c.--</hi>Speak proudly (Ob 12; <reference osisRef="Ezek.35.13">Eze 35:13</reference>).<div eID="gen7093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7094" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">against me--</hi>emphatically repeated (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.16">Psa 38:16</reference>).<div eID="gen7094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7095" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">plead ... reproach--</hi>English Version makes this part of the protasis, "if" being understood, and the apodosis beginning at <reference osisRef="Job.19.6">Job 19:6</reference>. Better with Umbreit, If ye would become great heroes against me in truth, ye must prove (evince) against me my guilt, or shame, which you assert. In the English Version "reproach" will mean Job's calamities, which they "pleaded" against him as a "reproach," or proof of guilt. <div eID="gen7095" type="x-p"/>
entries.368c11b4fef0b4890f43f0d5ad9081ef4e7cb277: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4848"/><div sID="gen7096" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4848"/><hi type="bold">6. compassed ... net--</hi>alluding to Bildad's words (<reference osisRef="Job.18.8">Job 18:8</reference>). Know, that it is not that I as a wicked man have been caught in my "own net"; it is God who has compassed me in His--why, I know not. <div eID="gen7096" type="x-p"/>
entries.eceac4edf0f4f4adcfb838c8e7d35f377cc249aa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4849"/><div sID="gen7097" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4849"/><hi type="bold">7. wrong--</hi>violence: brought on him by God.<div eID="gen7097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7098" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no judgment--</hi>God will not remove my calamities, and so vindicate my just cause; and my friends will not do justice to my past character. <div eID="gen7098" type="x-p"/>

entries.93a72fbfbd0d25e4e0c1d5660b5088c2da96a158: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4851"/><div sID="gen7100" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4851"/><hi type="bold">9. stripped ... crown--</hi>image from a deposed king, deprived of his robes and crown; appropriate to Job, once an emir with all but royal dignity (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.16">La 5:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.39">Psa 89:39</reference>). <div eID="gen7100" type="x-p"/>
entries.abbc8550f6bf9466881ca2b9f2e1fad51f1cb64b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4852"/><div sID="gen7101" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4852"/><hi type="bold">10. destroyed ... on every side--</hi>"Shaken all round, so that I fall in the dust"; image from a tree uprooted by violent shaking from every side [Umbreit]. The last clause accords with this (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.10">Jr 1:10</reference>)<div eID="gen7101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7102" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mine hope--</hi>as to this life (in opposition to Zophar, <reference osisRef="Job.11.18">Job 11:18</reference>); not as to the world to come (<reference osisRef="Job.19.25">Job 19:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.14.15">Job 14:15</reference>).<div eID="gen7102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7103" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">removed--</hi>uprooted. <div eID="gen7103" type="x-p"/>

entries.add2327b6971ba9886d8975e43be4e4e9377bace: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4854"/><div sID="gen7105" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4854"/><hi type="bold">12. troops--</hi>Calamities advance together like hostile troops (<reference osisRef="Job.10.17">Job 10:17</reference>).<div eID="gen7105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7106" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">raise up ... way--</hi>An army must cast up a way of access before it, in marching against a city (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.3">Is 40:3</reference>). <div eID="gen7106" type="x-p"/>
entries.111f52f215463d97806bb262798223773563e5e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4855"/><div sID="gen7107" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4855"/><hi type="bold">13. brethren--</hi>nearest kinsmen, as distinguished from "acquaintance." So "kinsfolk" and "familiar friends" (<reference osisRef="Job.19.14">Job 19:14</reference>) correspond in parallelism. The Arabic proverb is, "The brother, that is, the true friend, is only known in time of need."<div eID="gen7107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7108" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">estranged--</hi>literally, "turn away with disgust." Job again unconsciously uses language prefiguring the desertion of Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Job.16.10">Job 16:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.23.49">Lu 23:49</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.38.11">Psa 38:11</reference>). <div eID="gen7108" type="x-p"/>
entries.6d888f14cb9d3420d7d48cd83387bce04616a937: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4856"/><div sID="gen7109" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4856"/><hi type="bold">15. They that dwell, &c.--</hi>rather, "sojourn": male servants, sojourning in his house. Mark the contrast. The stranger admitted to sojourn as a dependent treats the master as a stranger in his own house. <div eID="gen7109" type="x-p"/>
entries.351ef12e22aaa53b59b4c8efddecafe58c293528: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4857"/><div sID="gen7110" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4857"/><hi type="bold">16. servant--</hi>born in my house (as distinguished from those sojourning in it), and so altogether belonging to the family. Yet even he disobeys my call.<div eID="gen7110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7111" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mouth--</hi>that is, "calling aloud"; formerly a nod was enough. Now I no longer look for obedience, I try entreaty. <div eID="gen7111" type="x-p"/>
entries.79c7119a696aad7fcddd83dcd282df9ce64c1caf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4858"/><div sID="gen7112" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4858"/><hi type="bold">17. strange--</hi>His breath by elephantiasis had become so strongly altered and offensive, that his wife turned away as estranged from him (<reference osisRef="Job.19.13">Job 19:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.17.1">17:1</reference>).<div eID="gen7112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7113" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">children's ... of mine own body--</hi>literally, "belly." But "loins" is what we should expect, not "belly" (womb), which applies to the woman. The "mine" forbids it being taken of his wife. Besides their children were dead. In <reference osisRef="Job.3.10">Job 3:10</reference> the same words "my womb" mean, my mother's womb: <hi type="bold">therefore translate, "and I must entreat (as a suppliant) the children of my mother's womb"; that is, my own brothers--</hi>a heightening of force, as compared with last clause of <reference osisRef="Job.19.16">Job 19:16</reference> [Umbreit]. Not only must I entreat suppliantly my servant, but my own brothers (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.8">Psa 69:8</reference>). Here too, he unconsciously foreshadows Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="John.7.5">Joh 7:5</reference>). <div eID="gen7113" type="x-p"/>
entries.96a3dc30f0a7eacf2ae063b66528f337e9aa16f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4859"/><div sID="gen7114" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4859"/><hi type="bold">18. young children--</hi>So the Hebrew means (<reference osisRef="Job.21.11">Job 21:11</reference>). Reverence for age is a chief duty in the East. The word means "wicked" (<reference osisRef="Job.16.11">Job 16:11</reference>). So Umbreit has it here, not so well.<div eID="gen7114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7115" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I arose--</hi>Rather, supply "if," as Job was no more in a state to stand up. "If I stood up (arose), they would speak against (abuse) me" [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen7115" type="x-p"/>
entries.2f834e2a1f1b555528f29ca358cddca60ac7b5e8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4860"/><div sID="gen7116" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4860"/><hi type="bold">19. inward--</hi>confidential; literally, "men of my secret"--to whom I entrusted my most intimate confidence. <div eID="gen7116" type="x-p"/>
entries.7b3816a02c7d8383699b603ee00f01da21af3bd1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4861"/><div sID="gen7117" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4861"/>20. Extreme meagerness. The bone seemed to stick in the skin, being seen through it, owing to the flesh drying up and falling away from the bone. The Margin, "as to my flesh," makes this sense clearer. The English Version, however, expresses the same: "And to my flesh," namely, which has fallen away from the bone, instead of firmly covering it.<div eID="gen7117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7118" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">skin of my teeth--</hi>proverbial. I have escaped with bare life; I am whole only with the skin of my teeth; that is, my gums alone are whole, the rest of the skin of my body is broken with sores (<reference osisRef="Job.7.5">Job 7:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.102.5">Psa 102:5</reference>). Satan left Job his speech, in hope that he might therewith curse God. <div eID="gen7118" type="x-p"/>
entries.1e04c4ca21175d476ee3c402bc06d2945c161058: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4862"/><div sID="gen7119" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4862"/>21. When God had made him such a piteous spectacle, his friends should spare him the additional persecution of their cruel speeches. <div eID="gen7119" type="x-p"/>
entries.5e27daf0dbf9901375d16d21f950047474dc8264: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4863"/><div sID="gen7120" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4863"/><hi type="bold">22. as God--</hi>has persecuted me. Prefiguring Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.26">Psa 69:26</reference>). That God afflicts is no reason that man is to add to a sufferer's affliction (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.15">Zec 1:15</reference>).<div eID="gen7120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7121" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">satisfied with my flesh--</hi>It is not enough that God afflicts my flesh literally (<reference osisRef="Job.19.20">Job 19:20</reference>), but you must "eat my flesh" metaphorically (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.2">Psa 27:2</reference>); that is, utter the worst calumnies, as the phrase often means in Arabic. <div eID="gen7121" type="x-p"/>
entries.16fb0341bd3838bf7d304a279d56ec36ac5f1f1b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4864"/><div sID="gen7122" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4864"/>23. Despairing of justice from his friends in his lifetime, he wishes his words could be preserved imperishably to posterity, attesting his hope of vindication at the resurrection.<div eID="gen7122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7123" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">printed--</hi>not our modern printing, but engraven. <div eID="gen7123" type="x-p"/>
entries.c5aa69f2374c6a0f41f971d801c017681df075ba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4865"/><div sID="gen7124" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4865"/><hi type="bold">24. pen--</hi>graver.<div eID="gen7124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7125" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lead--</hi>poured into the engraven characters, to make them better seen [Umbreit]. Not on leaden plates; for it was "in the rock" that they were engraved. Perhaps it was the hammer that was of "lead," as sculptors find more delicate incisions are made by it, than by a harder hammer. FOSTER (One Primeval Language) has shown that the inscriptions on the rocks in Wady-Mokatta, along Israel's route through the desert, record the journeys of that people, as Cosmas Indicopleustes asserted, A.D. 535.<div eID="gen7125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7126" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for ever--</hi>as long as the rock lasts. <div eID="gen7126" type="x-p"/>
entries.1adbd595d2da827667be24041ff6f89574c5e9c2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4866"/><div sID="gen7127" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4866"/><hi type="bold">25. redeemer--</hi>Umbreit and others understand this and <reference osisRef="Job.19.26">Job 19:26</reference>, of God appearing as Job's avenger before his death, when his body would be wasted to a skeleton. But Job uniformly despairs of restoration and vindication of his cause in this life (<reference osisRef="Job.17.15">Job 17:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.17.16">16</reference>). One hope alone was left, which the Spirit revealed--a vindication in a future life: it would be no full vindication if his soul alone were to be happy without the body, as some explain (<reference osisRef="Job.19.26">Job 19:26</reference>) "out of the flesh." It was his body that had chiefly suffered: the resurrection of his body, therefore, alone could vindicate his cause: to see God with his own eyes, and in a renovated body (<reference osisRef="Job.19.27">Job 19:27</reference>), would disprove the imputation of guilt cast on him because of the sufferings of his present body. That this truth is not further dwelt on by Job, or noticed by his friends, only shows that it was with him a bright passing glimpse of Old Testament hope, rather than the steady light of Gospel assurance; with us this passage has a definite clearness, which it had not in his mind (see on <reference osisRef="Job.21.30">Job 21:30</reference>). The idea in "redeemer" with Job is Vindicator (<reference osisRef="Job.16.19">Job 16:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.35.27">Nu 35:27</reference>), redressing his wrongs; also including at least with us, and probably with him, the idea of the predicted Bruiser of the serpent's head. Tradition would inform him of the prediction. Foster shows that the fall by the serpent is represented perfectly on the temple of Osiris at Philæ; and the resurrection on the tomb of the Egyptian Mycerinus, dating four thousand years back. Job's sacrifices imply sense of sin and need of atonement. Satan was the injurer of Job's body; Jesus Christ his Vindicator, the Living One who giveth life (<reference osisRef="John.5.21">Joh 5:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.26">26</reference>).<div eID="gen7127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7128" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at the latter day--</hi>Rather, "the Last," the peculiar title of Jesus Christ, though Job may not have known the pregnancy of his own inspired words, and may have understood merely one that comes after (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.45">1Co 15:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.17">Re 1:17</reference>). Jesus Christ is the last. The day of Jesus Christ the last day (<reference osisRef="John.6.39">Joh 6:39</reference>).<div eID="gen7128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7129" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stand--</hi>rather, "arise": as God is said to "raise up" the Messiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jr 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.18.15">De 18:15</reference>).<div eID="gen7129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7130" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">earth--</hi>rather, "dust": often associated with the body crumbling away in it (<reference osisRef="Job.7.21">Job 7:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.17.16">17:16</reference>); therefore appropriately here. Above that very dust wherewith was mingled man's decaying body shall man's Vindicator arise. "Arise above the dust," strikingly expresses that fact that Jesus Christ arose first Himself above the dust, and then is to raise His people above it (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.20">1Co 15:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.23">23</reference>). The Spirit intended in Job's words more than Job fully understood (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.12">1Pe 1:12</reference>). Though He seems, in forsaking me, to be as one dead, He now truly "liveth" in heaven; hereafter He shall appear also above the dust of earth. The Goel or vindicator of blood was the nearest kinsman of the slain. So Jesus Christ took our flesh, to be our kinsman. Man lost life by Satan the "murderer" (<reference osisRef="John.8.44">Joh 8:44</reference>), here Job's persecutor (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">He 2:14</reference>). Compare also as to redemption of the inheritance by the kinsman of the dead (<reference osisRef="Ruth.4.3-Ruth.4.5">Ru 4:3-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.14">Ep 1:14</reference>). <div eID="gen7130" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ec67797de5708375ee3e2ffad9422be50145bc1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4867"/><div sID="gen7131" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4867"/>26. Rather, though after my skin (is no more) this (body) is destroyed ("body" being omitted, because it was so wasted as not to deserve the name), yet from my flesh (from my renewed body, as the starting-point of vision, <reference osisRef="Song.2.9">So 2:9</reference>, "looking out from the windows") "shall I see God." Next clause [Job 19:27] proves bodily vision is meant, for it specifies "mine eyes" [Rosenmuller, 2d ed.]. The Hebrew opposes "in my flesh." The "skin" was the first destroyed by elephantiasis, then the "body." <div eID="gen7131" type="x-p"/>
entries.b2ab44ef872eb5b9bcae64d9130a8f2eb811341a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4868"/><div sID="gen7132" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4868"/><hi type="bold">27. for myself--</hi>for my advantage, as my friend.<div eID="gen7132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7133" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not another--</hi>Mine eyes shall behold Him, but no longer as one estranged from me, as now [Bengel].<div eID="gen7133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7134" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">though--</hi>better omitted.<div eID="gen7134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7135" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my reins--</hi>inward recesses of the heart.<div eID="gen7135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7136" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be consumed within me--</hi>that is, pine with longing desire for that day (<reference osisRef="Ps.84.2">Psa 84:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.81">119:81</reference>). The Gentiles had but few revealed promises: how gracious that the few should have been so explicit (compare <reference osisRef="Num.24.17">Nu 24:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.2.2">Mt 2:2</reference>). <div eID="gen7136" type="x-p"/>
entries.8b8cdeb3643be9b94e4a32aa81112d6edda0a971: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4869"/><div sID="gen7137" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4869"/>28. Rather, "ye will then (when the Vindicator cometh) say, Why," &c.<div eID="gen7137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7138" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">root ... in me--</hi>The root of pious integrity, which was the matter at issue, whether it could be in one so afflicted, is found in me. Umbreit, with many manuscripts and versions, reads "in him." "Or how found we in him ground of contention." <div eID="gen7138" type="x-p"/>
entries.802ff11cc65ffee39e4eb8a39c63b07a79164edc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4870"/><div sID="gen7139" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4870"/><hi type="bold">29. wrath--</hi>the passionate violence with which the friends persecuted Job.<div eID="gen7139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7140" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bringeth, &c.--</hi>literally, "is sin of the of the sword"<div eID="gen7140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7141" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that ye may know--</hi>Supply, "I say this."<div eID="gen7141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7142" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgment--</hi>inseparably connected with the coming of the Vindicator. The "wrath" of God at His appearing for the temporal vindication of Job against the friends (<reference osisRef="Job.42.7">Job 42:7</reference>) is a pledge of the eternal wrath at the final coming to glorify the saints and judge their enemies (<reference osisRef="2Thess.1.6-2Thess.1.10">2Th 1:6-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.25.8">Is 25:8</reference>). <chapter eID="Job.19"/>

entries.a61c34d8639007b8abee69457f22414e6c8d966a: <div eID="gen16750" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen16751" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16752" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16752" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16751" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16753" type="x-p"/> Job complains of the cruelty of his friends, <reference osisRef="Job.19.1-Job.19.5">Job 19:1-5</reference>. Pathetically laments his sufferings, <reference osisRef="Job.19.6-Job.19.12">Job 19:6-12</reference>. Complains of his being forsaken by all his domestics, friends, relatives, and even his wife, <reference osisRef="Job.19.13-Job.19.19">Job 19:13-19</reference>. Details his sufferings in an affecting manner, calls upon his friends to pity him, and earnestly wishes that his speeches may be recorded, <reference osisRef="Job.19.20-Job.19.24">Job 19:20-24</reference>. Expresses his hope in a future resurrection, <reference osisRef="Job.19.25-Job.19.27">Job 19:25-27</reference>. And warns his persecutors to desist, lest they fall under God's judgments, <reference osisRef="Job.19.28">Job 19:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.19.29">Job 19:29</reference>.
entries.dc8c04d054707f1c58b5d8be7cf0524672251683: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen16753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16754" type="x-p"/> How long will ye vex my soul - Every thing that was irritating, vexatious, and opprobrious, his friends had recourse to, in order to support their own system, and overwhelm him. Not one of them seems to have been touched with a feeling of tenderness towards him, nor does a kind expression drop at any time from their lips! They were called friends; but this term, in reference to them, must be taken in the sense of cold-blooded acquaintances. However, there are many in the world that go under the sacred name of friends, who, in times of difficulty, act a similar part. Job's friends have been, by the general consent of posterity, consigned to endless infamy. May all those who follow their steps be equally enrolled in the annals of bad fame!
entries.d993f3b9459195947b58b6ad1019b98c198cbc49: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen16754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16755" type="x-p"/> These ten times - The exact arithmetical number is not to be regarded; ten times being put for many times, as we have already seen. See particularly the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.31.7">Gen 31:7</reference> (note). <div eID="gen16755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16756" type="x-p"/> Ye make yourselves strange to me - When I was in affluence and prosperity, ye were my intimates, and appeared to rejoice in my happiness; but now ye scarcely know me, or ye profess to consider me a wicked man because I am in adversity. Of this you had no suspicion when I was in prosperity! Circumstances change men's minds.
entries.64ee86faca6c38c4cd398dec18b8fa326589e704: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen16756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16757" type="x-p"/> And be it indeed that I have erred - Suppose indeed that I have been mistaken in any thing, that in the simplicity of my heart I have gone astray, and that this matter remains with myself, (for most certainly there is no public stain on my life), you must grant that this error, whatsoever it is, has hurt no person except myself. Why then do ye treat me as a person whose life has been a general blot, and whose example must be a public curse?
entries.37aa1d8866ecadd1bd9658874c301e55232f7f07: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen16757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16758" type="x-p"/> Know now that God hath overthrown me - The matter is between him and me, and he has not commissioned you to add reproaches to his chastisements. <div eID="gen16758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16759" type="x-p"/> And hath compassed me with his net - There may be an allusion here to the different modes of hunting which have been already referred to in the preceding chapter. But if we take the whole verse together, and read the latter clause before the former, thus, "Know, therefore, that God hath encompassed me with his net, and overthrown me;" the allusion may be to an ancient mode of combat practiced among the ancient Persians, ancient Goths, and among the Romans. The custom among the Romans was this: "One of the combatants was armed with a sword and shield, the other with a trident and net. The net he endeavored to cast over the head of his adversary, in which, when he succeeded, the entangled person was soon pulled down by a noose that fastened round the neck, and then despatched. The person who carried the net and trident was called Retiarius, and the other who carried the sword and shield was termed Secutor, or the pursuer, because, when the Retiarius missed his throw, he was obliged to run about the ground till he got his net in order for a second throw, while the Secutor followed hard to prevent and despatch him." The Persians in old times used what was called (Persic) kumund, the noose. It was not a net, but a sort of running loop, which horsemen endeavored to cast over the heads of their enemies that they might pull them off their horses. That the Goths used a hoop net fastened to a pole, which they endeavored to throw over the heads of their foes, is attested by Olaus Magnus, Hist. de Gentibus Septentrionalibus, Rom. 1555, lib. xi., cap. 13, De diversis Modis praeliandi Finnorum. His words are, Quidam restibus instar retium ferinorum ductilibus sublimi jactatione utuntur: ubi enim cum hoste congressi sunt, injiciunt eos restes quasi laqueos in caput resistentis, ut equum aut hominem ad se trahant. "Some use elastic ropes, formed like hunting nets, which they throw aloft; and when they come in contact with the enemy, they throw these ropes over the head of their opponent, and by this means they can then drag either man or horse to themselves." At the head of the page he gives a wood-cut representing the net, and the manner of throwing it over the head of the enemy. To such a device Job might allude, God hath encompassed me with his Net, and overthrown me.
entries.887f4039c2151156e9d77a58e966786045fc5611: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen16759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16760" type="x-p"/> I cry out of wrong - I complain of violence and of injustice; but no one comes to my help.
entries.7230e07da8f13bae4df7e963b24f2125cb9b8875: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen16760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16761" type="x-p"/> He hath fenced up my way - This may allude to the mode of hunting the elephant, described at the conclusion of the preceding chapter; or to the operations of an invading army. See under <reference osisRef="Job.19.11">Job 19:11</reference> (note).
entries.6d3c75bf6a96f14ebd1c1e72c0f19298ddd52dfd: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen16761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16762" type="x-p"/> He hath stripped me of my glory - I am reduced to such circumstances, that I have lost all my honor and respect.
entries.006af94ff8ceab1589a60b286c963fcacd79b09d: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen16762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16763" type="x-p"/> Mine hope hath he removed like a tree - There is no more hope of my restoration to affluence, authority, and respect, than there is that a tree shall grow and flourish, whose roots are extracted from the earth. I am pulled up by the roots, withered, and gone.
entries.56c5558ed42ab23b6f2d80642a6f1d37607f36f2: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen16763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16764" type="x-p"/> And he counteth me unto him as one of his enemies - From the seventh to the thirteenth verse there seems to be an allusion to a hostile invasion, battles, sieges, etc. <div eID="gen16764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16765" type="x-p"/> 1. A neighboring chief, without provocation, invades his neighbor's territories, and none of his friends will come to his help. "I cry out of wrong, but I am not heard," <reference osisRef="Job.19.7">Job 19:7</reference>. <div eID="gen16765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16766" type="x-p"/> 2. The foe has seized on all the passes, and he is hemmed up. "He hath fenced up my way that I cannot pass," <reference osisRef="Job.19.8">Job 19:8</reference>. <div eID="gen16766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16767" type="x-p"/> 3. He has surprised and carried by assault the regal city, seized and possessed the treasures. "He hath stripped me of my glory, and taken the crown from my head," <reference osisRef="Job.19.9">Job 19:9</reference>. <div eID="gen16767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16768" type="x-p"/> 4. All his armies are routed in the field, and his strong places carried. "He hath destroyed me on every side," <reference osisRef="Job.19.10">Job 19:10</reference>. <div eID="gen16768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16769" type="x-p"/> 5. The enemy proceeds to the greatest length of outrage, wasting every thing with fire and sword. "He hath kindled his wrath against me, and treateth me like one of his adversaries, <reference osisRef="Job.19.11">Job 19:11</reference>. <div eID="gen16769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16770" type="x-p"/> 6. He is cooped up in a small camp with the wrecks of his army; and in this he is closely besieged by all the power of his foes, who encompass the place, and raise forts against it. "His troops come together, and raise up their way against me, and encamp round about my tabernacle." <div eID="gen16770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16771" type="x-p"/> 7. Not receiving any assistance from friends or neighbors, he abandons all hope of being able to keep the field, escapes with the utmost difficulty, and is despised and neglected by his friends and domestics because he has been unfortunate. "I am escaped with the skin of my teeth," <reference osisRef="Job.19.20">Job 19:20</reference>. "My kinsfolk have failed-all my intimate friends abhorred me," <reference osisRef="Job.19.14-Job.19.19">Job 19:14-19</reference>.
entries.fae760a11d033d8d3a50257101c23c142218bd5d: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen16771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16772" type="x-p"/> My kinsfolk have failed - Literally, departed: they have all left my house, now there is no more hope of gain.
entries.7d863c474398aafd1e1387f14140e0ebdb0261cc: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen16772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16773" type="x-p"/> They that dwell in mine house - In this and the following verses the disregard and contempt usually shown to men who have fallen from affluence and authority into poverty and dependence, are very forcibly described: formerly reverenced by all, now esteemed by none. Pity to those who have fallen into adversity is rarely shown; the rich have many friends, and to him who appears to be gaining worldly substance much court is paid; for many worship the rising sun, who think little of that which is gone down.
