Some are even reproached with that eminence which they have lost, though not culpable for the loss. A bishop, perhaps Bale, of Ossory, being obliged to leave his country and fly for his life, in the days of bloody Queen Mary, and who never regained his bishopric, was met one morning by one like those whom Job describes, who, intending to be witty at the expense of the venerable prelate, accosted him thus: "Good morrow, Bishop quondam." To which the bishop smartly replied, "Adieu, Knave semper."
entries.756246b8c4f6ab073090b6d5c4b05baa640cddb0: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen16773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16774" type="x-p"/> Though I entreated for the children's sake of mine own body - This may imply no more than adjuring her by the tenderest ties, by their affectionate intercourse, and consequently by the children which had been the seals of their mutual affection, though these children were no more. But the mention of his children in this place may intimate that he had still some remaining; that there might have been young ones, who, not being of a proper age to attend the festival of their elder brothers and sisters, escaped that sad catastrophe. The Septuagint have, Προσεκαλουμην δε κολακευων υἰους παλλακιδων μου, "I affectionately entreated the children of my concubines." But there is no ground in the Hebrew text for such a strange exceptionable rendering. Coverdale has, I am fayne to speake fayre to the children of myne own body.
entries.ab727347d247b75b32b49eda4c97fea62bcb2f8c: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen16774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16775" type="x-p"/> My inward friends - Those who were my greatest intimates.
entries.ea8588d4d8664867603a773f90dfc9e52ee2d3b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen16775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16776" type="x-p"/> My bone cleaveth to my skin - My flesh is entirely wasted away, and nothing but skin and bone left. <div eID="gen16776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16777" type="x-p"/> I am escaped with the skin of my teeth - I have had the most narrow escape. If I still live, it is a thing to be wondered at, my sufferings and privations have been so great. To escape with the skin of the teeth seems to have been a proverbial expression, signifying great difficulty. I had as narrow an escape from death, as the thickness of the enamel on the teeth. I was within a hair's breadth of destruction; see on <reference osisRef="Job.19.11">Job 19:11</reference> (note).
entries.ce5984dd0cb5a70a91aa7780a61221e078a8bee1: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen16777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16778" type="x-p"/> Have pity upon me - The iteration here strongly indicates the depth of his distress, and that his spirit was worn down with the length and severity of his suffering.
entries.7e9bc3c0a89bf0acff7665aae8e5a577f968f0a1: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen16778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16779" type="x-p"/> Why do ye persecute me as God - Are not the afflictions which God sends enough? Do ye not see that I have as much as I can bear? When the papists were burning Dr. Taylor at Oxford, while wrapped in the flames, one of the true sons of the Church took a stick out of the faggots, and threw it at his head, and split open his face. To whom he calmly said, Man, why this wrong? Do not I suffer enough? <div eID="gen16779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16780" type="x-p"/> And are not satisfied with my flesh? - Will ye persecute my soul, while God is persecuting my body? Is it not enough that my body is destroyed? Why then labor to torment my mind?
entries.e9aafb52f92711efb42595f19c5e197cbcb1f12d: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen16780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16781" type="x-p"/> O that my words were now written! - Job introduces the important subject which follows in a manner unusually solemn; and he certainly considers the words which he was about to utter of great moment, and therefore wishes them to be recorded in every possible way. All the modes of writing then in use he appears to refer to. As to printing, that should be out of the question, as no such art was then discovered, nor for nearly two thousand years after. Our translators have made a strange mistake by rendering the verb יחקו yuchaku, printed, when they should have used described, traced out. O that my words were fairly traced out in a book! It is necessary to make this remark, because superficial readers have imagined that the art of printing existed in Job's time, and that it was not a discovery of the fifteenth century of the Christian era: whereas there is no proof that it ever existed in the world before a.d. 1440, or thereabouts, for the first printed book with a date is a psalter printed by John Fust, in 1457, and the first Bible with a date is that by the same artist in 1460. Three kinds of writing Job alludes to, as being practiced in his time: <div eID="gen16781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16782" type="x-p"/> 1. Writing in a book, formed either of the leaves of the papyrus, already described, (see on <reference osisRef="Job.8.11">Job 8:11</reference> (note)), or on a sort of linen cloth. A roll of this kind, with unknown characters, I have seen taken out of the envelopments of an Egyptian mummy. Denon, in his travels in Egypt, gives an account of a book of this kind, with an engraved facsimile, taken also out of an Egyptian mummy. <div eID="gen16782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16783" type="x-p"/> 2. Cutting with an iron stile on plates of lead. <div eID="gen16783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16784" type="x-p"/> 3. Engraving on large stones or rocks, many of which are still found in different parts of Arabia. <div eID="gen16784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16785" type="x-p"/> To the present day the leaves of the palm tree are used in the East instead of paper, and a stile of brass, silver, iron, etc., with a steel point, serves for a pen. By this instrument the letters are cut or engraved on the substance of the leaf, and afterwards some black colouring matter is rubbed in, in order to make the letters apparent. This was probably the oldest mode of writing, and it continues among the Cingalese to the present day. It is worthy of remark that Pliny (Hist. Nat., lib. xiii., c. 11) mentions most of these methods of writing, and states that the leaves of the palm tree were used before other substances were invented. After showing that paper was not used before the conquest of Egypt by Alexander the Great, he proceeds: In palmarum foliis primo scriptitatum; deinde quarundam arborum libris: postea publica monumenta plumbeis voluminibus, mox et privata linteis confici caepta, aut ceris. "At first men wrote on palm tree leaves, and afterwards on the bark or rind of other trees. In process of time, public monuments were written on rolls of lead, and those of a private nature on linen books, or tables covered with wax." Pausanias, lib. xii., c. 31, giving an account of the Boeotians, who dwelt near fount Helicon, states the following fact: - Και μοι μολιβδον εδεικνυσαν, ενθα ἡ πηγη, τα πολλα ὑπο του χρονου λελυμασμενον, εγγεγραπται γαρ αυτῳ τα εργα; "They showed me a leaden table near to the fountain, all which his works (Hesiod's) were written; but a great part had perished by the injuries of time."
entries.22a2330a0486fc21addfd5263b7b163005081271: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen16785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16786" type="x-p"/> Iron pen and lead - Some suppose that the meaning of this place is this: the iron pen is the chisel by which the letters were to be deeply cut in the stone or rock; and the lead was melted into those cavities in order to preserve the engraving distinct. But this is not so natural a supposition as what is stated above; that Job refers to the different kinds of writing or perpetuating public events, used in his time: and the quotations from Pliny and Pausanias confirm the opinion already expressed.
entries.541f72d7b633f8b1bc2f1bd9af75169bb659bdc6: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen16786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16787" type="x-p"/> For I know that my Redeemer liveth - Any attempt to establish the true meaning of this passage is almost hopeless. By learned men and eminent critics the words have been understood very differently; some vehemently contending that they refer to the resurrection of the body, and the redemption of the human race by Jesus Christ; while others, with equal vehemence and show of argument, have contended that they refer only to Job's restoration to health, family comforts, and general prosperity, after the present trial should be ended. In defense of these two opinions larger treatises have been written than the whole book of Job would amount to, if written even in capitals. To discuss the arguments on either side the nature of this work forbids; but my own view of the subject will be reasonably expected by the reader. I shall therefore lay down one principle, without which no mode of interpretation hitherto offered can have any weight. The principle is this: Job was now under the especial inspiration of the Holy Spirit, and spoke prophetically. Now, whether we allow that the passage refers to the general resurrection and the redemption by Christ, or to Job's restoration to health, happiness, and prosperity, this principle is equally necessary. <div eID="gen16787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16788" type="x-p"/> 1. In those times no man could speak so clearly concerning the general resurrection and the redemption by Jesus Christ as Job, by one class of interpreters, is supposed here to do, unless especially inspired for this very purpose. <div eID="gen16788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16789" type="x-p"/> 2. Job's restoration to health and happiness, which, though it did take place, was so totally improbable to himself all the way through, so wholly unexpected, and, in every sense, impossible, except to the almighty power of God, that it could not be inferred from any thing that had already taken place, and must be foreshown by direct inspiration. <div eID="gen16789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16790" type="x-p"/> Now, that it was equally easy to predict either of these events, will be at once evident, because both were in futurity, and both were previously determined. Nothing contingent could exist in either; with them man had nothing to do; and they were equally within the knowledge of Him to whose ubiquity there can be neither past nor future time; in whose presence absolute and contingent events subsist in their own distinctive characters, and are never resolved into each other. But another question may arise, Which was most likely to be the subject of this oracular declaration, the general resurrection and redemption by Christ; or the restoration of Job to health and affluence? If we look only to the general importance of these things, this question may be soon decided; for the doctrine of human redemption, and the general resurrection to an eternal life, are of infinitely greater importance than any thing that could affect the personal welfare of Job. We may therefore say, of two things which only the power of God can effect, and one of which only shall be done it is natural to conclude he will do that which is of most importance; and that is of most importance by which a greater measure of glory is secured to himself, and a greater sum of good produced to mankind. As, therefore, a revelation by which the whole human race, in all its successive generations, to the end of time, may be most essentially benefited, is superior in its worth and importance to that by which one man only can be benefited, it is natural to conclude here, that the revelation relative to the general resurrection, etc., is that which most likely the text includes. But to this it may be answered, God does not do always in the first instance that which is most necessary and important in itself, as every thing is done in that order and in that time which seems best to his godly wisdom; therefore, a thing of less importance may be done now, and a thing of greater importance left to a future time. So, God made the earth before he made man, produced light before he formed the celestial luminaries, and instituted the Mosaic economy before the Christian dispensation. This is all true, for every thing is done in that season in which it may best fulfill the designs of providence and grace. But the question still recurs, Which of the predictions was most congruous to the circumstances of Job, and those of his companions; and which of them was most likely to do most good on that occasion, and to be most useful through the subsequent ages of the world? The subject is now considerably narrowed; and, if this question could be satisfactorily answered, the true meaning of the passage would be at once found out. <div eID="gen16790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16791" type="x-p"/> 1. For the sake of righteousness, justice, and truth, and to vindicate the ways of God with man, it was necessary that Job's innocence should be cleared; that the false judgments of his friends should be corrected; and that, as Job was now reduced to a state of the lowest distress, it was worthy the kindness of God to give him some direct intimation that his sufferings should have a happy termination. That such an event ought to take place, there can be no question: and that it did take place, is asserted in the book; and that Job's friends saw it, were reproved, corrected, and admitted into his favor of whom they did not speak that which was right, and who had, in consequence, God's wrath kindled against them, are also attested facts. But surely there was no need of so solemn a revelation to inform them of what was shortly to take place, when they lived to see it; nor can it be judged essentially necessary to the support of Job, when the ordinary consolations of God's Spirit, and the excitement of a good hope through grace, might have as completely answered the end. <div eID="gen16791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16792" type="x-p"/> 2. On the other hand, to give men, who were the chiefs of their respective tribes, proper notice of a doctrine of which they appear to have had no adequate conception, and which was so necessary to the peace of society, the good government of men, and the control of unruly and wayward passions, which the doctrine of the general resurrection and consequent judgment is well calculated to produce; and to stay and support the suffering godly under the afflictions and calamities of life; were objects worthy the highest regards of infinite philanthropy and justice, and of the most pointed and solemn revelation which could be given on such an occasion. In short, they are the grounds on which all revelation is given to the sons of men: and the prophecy in question, viewed in this light, was, in that dark age and country, a light shining in a dark place; for the doctrine of the general resurrection and of future rewards and punishments, existed among the Arabs from time immemorial, and was a part of the public creed of the different tribes when Mohammed endeavored to establish his own views of that resurrection and of future rewards and punishments, by the edge of the sword. I have thus endeavored dispassionately to view this subject; and having instituted the preceding mode of reasoning, without foreseeing where it would tend, being only desirous to find out truth, I arrive at the conclusion, that the prophecy in question was not designed to point out the future prosperity of Job; but rather the future redemption of mankind by Jesus Christ, and the general resurrection of the human race. After what has been stated above, a short paraphrase on the words of the text will be all that is necessary to be added. I know, ידעתי yadati, I have a firm and full persuasion, that my Redeemer, גאלי goali, my Kinsman, he whose right it was among the ancient Hebrews to redeem the forfeited heritages belonging to the family, to vindicate its honor, and to avenge the death of any of his relatives by slaying the murderer; (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.25">Lev 25:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.35.12">Num 35:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rut.3.13">Rut 3:13</reference>); but here it must refer to Christ, who has truly the right of redemption, being of the same kindred, who was born of woman, flesh of flesh and bone of our bone. Liveth, חי chai, is the living One, who has the keys of hell and death: the Creator and Lord of the spirits of all flesh, and the principle and support of all life. And that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth. The latter day, אחרון acharon, the latter day, or time, when God comes to judgment; or finally, or at last, or in the last time, or latter days, as the Gospel is termed, he shall be manifested in the flesh. He shall stand, יקום yakum, he shall arise, or stand up, i.e., to give sentence in judgment: or he himself shall arise from the dust, as the passage has been understood by some to refer to the resurrection of Christ from the dead. Upon the earth, על עפר al aphar, over the dead, or those who are reduced to dust. This is the meaning of עפר aphar in <reference osisRef="Psa.30.9">Psa 30:9</reference> : What profit is there in my blood when I go down to the pit? Shall the Dust (i.e., the dead) praise thee? He shall arise over the dust - over them who sleep in the dust, whom he shall also raise up.
entries.d9f2176664a191bf3c8ac92b2f74d83ad07ae39c: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen16792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16793" type="x-p"/> And though after my skin worms destroy this body - My skin, which is now almost all that remains of my former self, except the bones; see <reference osisRef="Job.19.20">Job 19:20</reference>. They destroy this - not body. נקפו זאת nikkephu zoth, they - diseases and affliction, destroy This wretched composition of misery and corruption. <div eID="gen16793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16794" type="x-p"/> Yet in my flesh shall I see God - Either, I shall arise from the dead, have a renewed body and see him with eyes of flesh and blood, though what I have now shall shortly moulder into dust, or, I shall see him in the flesh; my Kinsman, who shall partake of my flesh and blood, in order that he may ransom the lost inheritance.
entries.92c7fe8a52f34f552387a242169499f04be63751: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen16794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16795" type="x-p"/> Whom I shall see for myself - Have a personal interest in the resurrection, as I shall have in the Redeemer. <div eID="gen16795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16796" type="x-p"/> And mine eyes shall behold - That very person who shall be the resurrection, as he is the life. <div eID="gen16796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16797" type="x-p"/> And not another - ולא זר velo zar, and not a stranger, one who has no relation to human nature; but גאלי goali, my redeeming Kinsman. <div eID="gen16797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16798" type="x-p"/> Though my reins be consumed within me - Though I am now apparently on the brink of death, the thread of life being spun out to extreme tenuity. This, on the mode of interpretation which I have assumed, appears to be the meaning of this passage. The words may have a somewhat different colouring put on them; but the basis of the interpretation will be the same. I shall conclude with the version of Coverdale: - <div eID="gen16798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16799" type="x-p"/> For I am sure that my Redeemer liveth; <div eID="gen16799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16800" type="x-p"/> And that I shal ryse out of the earth in the latter daye; <div eID="gen16800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16801" type="x-p"/> That I shal be clothed againe with this skynne <div eID="gen16801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16802" type="x-p"/> And se God in my flesh. <div eID="gen16802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16803" type="x-p"/> Yee, I myself shal beholde him, <div eID="gen16803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16804" type="x-p"/> Not with other, but with these same eyes. <div eID="gen16804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16805" type="x-p"/> My reins are consumed within me, when ye saye, <div eID="gen16805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16806" type="x-p"/> Why do not we persecute him? <div eID="gen16806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16807" type="x-p"/> We have founde an occasion against him.
entries.714c9404e61ca9713db41211b5dd30201ceba993: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen16807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16808" type="x-p"/> But ye should say - Or, Then ye shall say. <div eID="gen16808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16809" type="x-p"/> Why persecute we him - Or, as Mr. Good, How did we persecute him! Alas! we are now convinced that we did wrong. <div eID="gen16809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16810" type="x-p"/> Seeing the root of the matter - A pure practice, and a sound hope, resting on the solid ground of sound faith, received from God himself. Instead of בי bi, in Me, בי bo, in Him, is the reading of more than one hundred of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., and in several of the versions. Seeing the root of the matter is found in Him.
entries.58f6a41ebce5b5862a3f1eeec41d67f6302479ec: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen16810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16811" type="x-p"/> Be ye afraid of the sword - Of God's judgments. <div eID="gen16811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16812" type="x-p"/> For wrath bringeth - Such anger as ye have displayed against me, God will certainly resent and punish. <div eID="gen16812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16813" type="x-p"/> That ye may know there is a judgment - That ye may know that God will judge the world; and that the unequal distribution of riches and poverty, afflictions and health, in the present life, is a proof that there must be a future judgment, where evil shall be punished and virtue rewarded. <div eID="gen16813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16814" type="x-p"/> It would not be fair, after all the discussion of the preceding verses in reference to the two grand opinions and modes of interpretation instituted by learned men, not to inform the reader that a third method of solving all difficulties has been proposed, viz., that Job refers to a Divine conviction which he had just then received, that God would appear in the most evident manner to vindicate his innocence, and give the fullest proofs to his friends and to the world that his afflictions had not been sent as a scourge for his iniquities. Dr. Kennicott was the proposer of this third mode of solving these difficulties, and I shall give his method in his own words. "These five verses, though they contain but twelve lines, have occasioned controversies without number, as to the general meaning of Job in this place, whether he here expressed his firm belief of a resurrection to happiness after death, or of a restoration to prosperity during the remainder of his life. "Each of these positions has found powerful as well as numerous advocates; and the short issue of the whole seems to be, that each party has confuted the opposite opinion, yet without establishing its own. For how could Job here express his conviction of a reverse of things in this world, and of a restoration to temporal prosperity, at the very time when he strongly asserts that his miseries would soon be terminated by death? See <reference osisRef="Job.6.11">Job 6:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.7.21">Job 7:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.17.11-Job.17.15">Job 17:11-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.19.10">Job 19:10</reference>, and particularly in <reference osisRef="Job.7.7">Job 7:7</reference> : O remember that my life is wind; mine eye shall no more see good. "Still less could Job here express a hope full of immortality, which sense cannot be extorted from the words without every violence. And as the possession of such belief is not to be reconciled with Job's so bitterly cursing the day of his birth in <reference osisRef="Job.3.1-Job.3.3">Job 3:1-3</reference>, so the declaration of such belief would have solved at once the whole difficulty in dispute. "But if neither of the preceding and opposite opinions can be admitted, if the words are not meant to express Job's belief either of a restoration or of a resurrection, what then are we to do? It does not appear to me that any other interpretation has yet been proposed by the learned; yet I will now venture to offer a third interpretation, different from both the former, and which, whilst it is free from the preceding difficulties, does not seem liable to equal objections. "The conviction, then, which I suppose Job to express here, is this: That though his dissolution was hastening on amidst the unjust accusations of his pretended friends, and the cruel insults of his hostile relations; and though, whilst he was thus singularly oppressed with anguish of mind, he was also tortured with pains of body, torn by sores and ulcers from head to foot, and sitting upon dust and ashes; yet still, out of that miserable body, in his flesh thus stripped of skin, and nearly dropping into the grave, He Should See God, who would appear in his favor, and vindicate The Integrity of his character. This opinion may perhaps be fairly and fully supported by the sense of the words themselves, by the context, and by the following remarks. "We read in <reference osisRef="Job.2.7">Job 2:7</reference>, that Job was smitten with sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown; and <reference osisRef="Job.2.8">Job 2:8</reference>, 'He sat down among the ashes.' In <reference osisRef="Job.7.5">Job 7:5</reference>, Job says, 'My flesh is clothed with worms, and clods of dust; my skin is broken, and become loathsome.' In <reference osisRef="Job.16.19">Job 16:19</reference> : 'Also now, behold, my witness is in heaven, and my record is on high.' Then come the words of Job, <reference osisRef="Job.19.25-Job.19.29">Job 19:25-29</reference>. And then, in opposition to what Job had just said, that God would soon appear to vindicate him, and that even his accusing friends would acquit him, Zophar says, <reference osisRef="Job.20.27">Job 20:27</reference>, that 'the heaven would reveal his iniquity, and the earth would rise up against him.' Lastly, this opinion concerning Job's words, as to God's vindication of him, is confirmed strongly at the end of the book, which records the conclusion of Job's history. His firm hope is here supposed to be that, before his death, he should, with his bodily eyes, see God appearing and vindicating his character. And from the conclusion we learn that God did thus appear: Now, says Job, mine eye seeth thee. And then did God most effectually and for ever brighten the glory of Job's fame, by four times calling him His Servant; and, as his anger was kindled against Job's friends, by speaking to them in the following words: 'Ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath. Go to my servant Job, - and my servant Job shall pray for you, - in that ye have not spoken of me the thing which is right, like my servant Job,' <reference osisRef="Job.40.7">Job 40:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.40.8">Job 40:8</reference>." Dr. K. then gives the common version, and proposes the following as a new version: - <reference osisRef="Job.19.25">Job 19:25</reference> For I know that my Vindicator liveth,And he at last shall arise over this dust. <reference osisRef="Job.19.26">Job 19:26</reference> And after that mine adversaries have mangled me thus,Even in my flesh shall I see God. <reference osisRef="Job.19.27">Job 19:27</reference> Whom I shall see on my side;And mine eyes shall behold, but not estranged from me:All this have I made up in mine bosom. <reference osisRef="Job.19.28">Job 19:28</reference> Verily ye shall say, Why have we persecuted him;Seeing the truth of the matter is found with him? <reference osisRef="Job.19.29">Job 19:29</reference> Tremble for yourselves at the face of the sword;For the sword waxeth hot against iniquities:Therefore be assured that judgment will take place. <div eID="gen16814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16815" type="x-p"/> Kennicott's Remarks on Select Passages of Scripture, p. 165. <div eID="gen16815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16816" type="x-p"/> There is something very plausible in this plan of Dr. Kennicott; and in the conflicting opinions relative to the meaning of this celebrated and much controverted passage, no doubt some will be found who will adopt it as a middle course. The theory, however, is better than some of the arguments by which it is supported. Yet had I not been led, by the evidence mentioned before, to the conclusion there drawn, I should probably have adopted Dr. K.'s opinion with some modification: but as to his new version, it is what I am persuaded the Hebrew text can never bear. It is even too loose a paraphrase of the original, as indeed are most of the new versions of this passage. Dr. Kennicott says, that such a confidence as those cause Job to express, who make him speak concerning the future resurrection, ill comports with his cursing so bitterly the day of his birth, etc. But this objection has little if any strength, when we consider that it is not at all probable that Job had this confidence any time before the moment in which he uttered it: it was then a direct revelation, nothing of which he ever had before, else he had never dropped those words of impatience and irritation which we find in several of his speeches. And this may be safely inferred from the consideration, that after this time no such words escaped his lips: he bears the rest of his sufferings with great patience and fortitude; and seems to look forward with steady hope to that day in which all tears shall be wiped away from off all faces, and it be fully proved that the Judge of all the earth has done right.  <chapter eID="Job.19"/> <div eID="gen16816" type="x-p"/>

entries.1782ee963eaf764acd58bcd2557914038e1ed59a: <reference osisRef="Job.19.1-Job.6.1">Job 19:1-6   1</reference>  Then began Job, and said:   2  How long will ye vex my soul, <div eID="gen7639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7640" type="x-p"/> And crush me with your words?   3  These ten times have ye reproached me; <div eID="gen7640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7641" type="x-p"/> Without being ashamed ye astound me.   4  And if I have really erred, <div eID="gen7641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7642" type="x-p"/> My error rests with myself.   5  If ye will really magnify yourselves against me, <div eID="gen7642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7643" type="x-p"/> And prove my reproach to me:   6 Know then that Eloah hath wronged me, <div eID="gen7643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7644" type="x-p"/> And hath compassed me with His net. <div eID="gen7644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7645" type="x-p"/> This controversy is torture to Job’s spirit; enduring in himself unutterable agony, both bodily and spiritually, and in addition stretched upon the rack by the three friends with their united strength, he begins his answer with a well-justified <hi type="italic">quousque tandem</hi>. תּגיוּן (Norzi: תּוגיוּן) is <hi type="italic">fut. energicum</hi> from הוּגה (יגה), with the retention of the third radical., Ges. §75, rem. 16. And in וּתדכּאוּנני (Norzi: וּתדכּוּנני with quiescent <hi type="italic">Aleph</hi>) the suff. is attached to the <hi type="italic">ûn</hi> of the <hi type="italic">fut. energicum</hi>, Ges. §60, rem. 3; the connecting vowel is <hi type="italic">a</hi>, and the suff. is <hi type="italic">ani</hi>, without epenthesis, not <hi type="italic">anni</hi> or <hi type="italic">aneni</hi>, Ges. §58, 5. In <reference osisRef="Job.19.3">Job 19:3</reference> Job establishes his How long? Ten times is not to be taken strictly (Saad.), but it is a round number; ten, from being the number of the fingers on the human hand, is the number of human possibility, and from its position at the end of the row of numbers (in the decimal system) is the number of that which is perfected (vid., <hi type="italic">Genesis</hi>, S. 640f.); as not only the Sanskrit <hi type="italic">daçan</hi> is traceable to the radical notion “to seize, embrace,” but also the Semitic עשר is traceable to the radical notion “to bind, gather together” (cogn. קשׁר). They have already exhausted what is possible in reproaches, they have done their utmost. Renan, in accordance with the Hebr. expression, transl.: <hi type="italic">Voilà</hi> (זה, as e.g., <reference osisRef="Gen.27.36">Gen 27:36</reference>) <hi type="italic">la dixième fois que vous m'insultez.</hi> The ἅπ. γεγρ. תּהכּרוּ is connected by the Targ. with הכּיר (of respect of persons = partiality), by the Syr. with כּרא (to pain, of <hi type="italic">crêvecoeur</hi>), by Raschi and Parchon with נכּר (to mistake) or התנכּר (to alienate one’s self), by Saadia (vid., Ewald’s <hi type="italic">Beitr</hi>. S. 99) with עכר (to dim, grieve);<note placement="foot">Reiske interprets according to the Arabic <hi type="italic">‛kr , denso et turbido agmine cum impetu ruitis in me.</hi></note> he, however, compares the Arab. <hi type="italic">hkr , stupere</hi> (which he erroneously regards as differing only in sound from Arab. <hi type="italic">qhr</hi>, to overpower, oppress); and Abulwalid (vid., Rödiger in <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. p. 84 <hi type="italic">suppl</hi>.) explains Arab. <hi type="italic">thkrûn mn - nı̂</hi>, ye gaze at me, since at the same time he mentions as possible that הכר may be = Arab. <hi type="italic">khr</hi>, to treat indignantly, insultingly (which is only a different shade in sound of Arab. <hi type="italic">hkr</hi>,<note placement="foot">In <hi type="italic">Sur</hi>. 93, 9 (oppress not the orphan), the reading Arab. <hi type="italic">tkhr</hi> is found alternating with Arab. <hi type="italic">tqhr</hi>.</note> and therefore refers to Saadia’s interpretation). David Kimchi interprets according to Abulwalid, תתמהו לו; he however remarks at the same time, that his father Jos. Kimchi interprets after the Arab. הכר, which also signifies “shamelessness,” תעיזו פניכם לי. Since the idea of dark wild looks is connected with Arab. <hi type="italic">hkr</hi>, he has undoubtedly this verb in his mind, not that compared by Ewald (who translates, “ye are devoid of feeling towards me”), and especially Arab. <hi type="italic">hkr</hi>, to deal unfairly, used of usurious trade in corn (which may also have been thought of by the lxx ἐπίκεισθέ μοι, and Jerome <hi type="italic">opprimentes</hi>), which signifies as intrans. to be obstinate about anything, pertinacious. Gesenius also, <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. p. 84, <hi type="italic">suppl.,</hi> suggests whether תּחכּרוּ may not perhaps be the reading. But the comparison with Arab. <hi type="italic">hkr</hi> is certainly safer, and gives a perfectly satisfactory meaning, only תּהכּרוּ must not be regarded as <hi type="italic">fut. Kal</hi> (as יהלם, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.6">Psa 74:6</reference>, according to the received text), but as <hi type="italic">fut. Hiph</hi>. for תּהכּירוּ, according to Ges. §53, rem. 4, 5, after which Schultens transl.: <hi type="italic">quod me ad stuporem redigatis.</hi> The connection of the two verbs in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.19.3">Job 19:3</reference></hi> is to be judged of according to Ges. §142, 3, <hi type="italic">a</hi>: ye shamelessly cause me astonishment (by the assurance of your accusations). One need not hesitate because it is תהכרו־לי instead of תהכרוני; this indication of the obj. by ל, which is become a rule in Arabic with the inf. and part.) whence e.g., it would here be <hi type="italic">muhkerina li</hi>), and is still more extended in Aramaic, is also frequent in Hebrew (e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">Isa 53:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.116.16">Psa 116:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.129.3">Psa 129:3</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.17">2Ch 32:17</reference>, cheereep, after which Olsh. proposes to read תחרפו־לי in the passage before us). <div eID="gen7645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7646" type="x-p"/> Much depends upon the correct perception of the structure of the clauses in Job 19:4. The rendering, e.g., of Olshausen, gained by taking the two halves of the verse as independent clauses, “yea certainly I have erred, I am fully conscious of my error,” puts a confession into Job’s mouth, which is at present neither mature nor valid. Hirz., Hahn, Schlottm., rightly take <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.19.4">Job 19:4</reference></hi> as a hypothetical antecedent clause (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.7.20">Job 7:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.11.18">Job 11:18</reference>): and if I have really erred (אף־אמנם, as <reference osisRef="Job.34.12">Job 34:12</reference>, yea truly; <reference osisRef="Gen.18.13">Gen 18:13</reference>, and if I should really), my error remains with me, i.e., I shall have to expiate it, without your having on this account any right to take upon yourselves the office of God and to treat me uncharitably; or what still better corresponds with תּלין אתּי: my transgression remains with me, without being communicated to another, i.e., without having any influence over you or others to lead you astray or involve you in participation of the guilt. <reference osisRef="Job.19.6">Job 19:6</reference> stands in a similar relation to Job 19:5. Hirz., Ew., and Hahn take <reference osisRef="Job.19.5">Job 19:5</reference> as a double question: “or will ye really boast against me, and prove to me my fault?” Schlottm., on the contrary, takes אם conditionally, and begins the conclusion with <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.19.5">Job 19:5</reference></hi>: “if ye will really look proudly down upon me, it rests with you at least, to prove to me by valid reasons, the contempt which ye attach to me.” But by both of these interpretations, especially by the latter, <reference osisRef="Job.19.6">Job 19:6</reference> comes in abruptly. Even אפו (written thus in three other passages besides this) indicates in <reference osisRef="Job.19.5">Job 19:5</reference> the conditional antecedent clause (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.9.24">Job 9:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.24.25">Job 24:25</reference>) of the expressive γνῶστε οὖν (δή): if ye really boast yourselves against me (vid., Psa 55:13., comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.35.26">Psa 35:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.38.17">Psa 38:17</reference>), and prove upon me, i.e., in a way of punishment (as ye think), my shame, i.e., the sins which put me to shame (not: the right of shame, which has come upon me on account of my sins, an interpretation which the conclusion does not justify), therefore: if ye really continue (which is implied by the <hi type="italic">futt.</hi>) to do this, then know, etc. If they really maintain that he is suffering on account of flagrant sins, he meets them on the ground of this assumption with the assertion that God has wronged him (עוּתני short for עוּת משׁפּטי, <reference osisRef="Job.8.3">Job 8:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.34.12">Job 34:12</reference>, as <reference osisRef="Lam.3.36">Lam 3:36</reference>), and has cast His net (מצוּדו, with the change of the <hi type="italic">ô</hi> of מצוד from צוּד, to search, hunt, into the deeper <hi type="italic">û</hi> in inflexion, as מנוּסי from מנוס, מצוּרך, <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.8">Eze 4:8</reference>, from מצור) over him, together with his right and his freedom, so that he is indeed obliged to endure punishment. In other words: if his suffering is really not to be regarded otherwise than as the punishment of sin, as they would uncharitably and censoriously persuade him, it urges on his self-consciousness, which rebels against it, to the conclusion which he hurls into their face as one which they themselves have provoked.
entries.37ef5a88b6e679dba1529d3eea75af3671b342d6: <reference osisRef="Job.19.7-Job.11.7">Job 19:7-11   7</reference>  Behold I cry violence, and I am not heard; <div eID="gen7646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7647" type="x-p"/> I cry for help, and there is no justice.   8  My way He hath fenced round, that I cannot pass over, <div eID="gen7647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7648" type="x-p"/> And He hath set darkness on my paths.   9  He hath stripped me of mine honour, <div eID="gen7648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7649" type="x-p"/> And taken away the crown from my head. 10  He destroyed me on every side, then I perished, <div eID="gen7649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7650" type="x-p"/> And lifted out as a tree my hope. 11  He kindled His wrath against me, <div eID="gen7650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7651" type="x-p"/> And He regarded me as one of His foes. <div eID="gen7651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7652" type="x-p"/> He cries aloud חמס (that which is called out regarded as <hi type="italic">accusa</hi>. or as an interjection, vid., on <reference osisRef="Hab.1.2">Hab 1:2</reference>), i.e., that illegal force is exercised over him. He finds, however, neither with God nor among men any response of sympathy and help; he cries for help (which שׁוּע, perhaps connected with ישׁע, Arab. <hi type="italic">s‛t</hi>, from ישׁע, Arab. <hi type="italic">ws‛</hi>, seems to signify), without justice, i.e., the right of an impartial hearing and verdict, being attainable by him. He is like a prisoner who is confined to a narrow space (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.3.23">Job 3:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.13.27">Job 13:27</reference>) and has no way out, since darkness is laid upon him wherever he may go. One is here reminded of <reference osisRef="Lam.3.7-Lam.3.9">Lam 3:7-9</reference>; and, in fact, this speech generally stands in no accidental mutual relation to the lamentations of Jeremiah. The “crown of my head” has also its parallel in <reference osisRef="Lam.5.16">Lam 5:16</reference>; that which was Job’s greatest ornament and most costly jewel is meant. According to <reference osisRef="Job.29.14">Job 29:14</reference>, צדק and משׁפט were his robe and diadem. These robes of honour God has stripped from him, this adornment more precious than a regal diadem He has taken from him since, i.e., his affliction puts him down as a transgressor, and abandons him to the insult of those around him. God destroyed him roundabout (<hi type="italic">destruxit</hi>), as a house that is broken down on all sides, and lifted out as a tree his hope. הסּיע does not in itself signify to root out, but only to lift out (<reference osisRef="Job.4.21">Job 4:21</reference>, of the tent-cord, and with it the tent-pin) of a plant: to remove it from the ground in which it has grown, either to plant it elsewhere, as <reference osisRef="Ps.80.9">Psa 80:9</reference>, or as here, to put it aside. The ground was taken away from his hope, so that its greenness faded away like that of a tree that is rooted up. The <hi type="italic">fut. consec.</hi> is here to be translated: then I perished (different from <reference osisRef="Job.14.20">Job 14:20</reference> : and consequently he perishes); he is now already one who is passed away, his existence is only the shadow of life. God has caused, <hi type="italic">fut. Hiph. apoc.</hi> ויּחר, His wrath to kindle against him, and regarded him in relation to Himself as His opponents, therefore as one of them. Perhaps, however, the expression is intentionally intensified here, in contrast with <reference osisRef="Job.13.24">Job 13:24</reference> : he, the one, is accounted by God as the host of His foes; He treats him as if all hostility to God were concentrated in him.
entries.a24aca56a8abcf7b401d624f84230c921f9e7fcc: <reference osisRef="Job.19.12-Job.15.12">Job 19:12-15 12</reference>  His troops came together, <div eID="gen7652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7653" type="x-p"/> And threw up their way against me, <div eID="gen7653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7654" type="x-p"/> And encamped round about my tent. 13  My brethren hath He removed far from me, <div eID="gen7654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7655" type="x-p"/> And my acquaintance are quite estranged from me. 14  My kinsfolk fail, <div eID="gen7655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7656" type="x-p"/> And those that knew me have forgotten me. 15  The slaves of my house and my maidens, <div eID="gen7656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7657" type="x-p"/> They regard me as a stranger, <div eID="gen7657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7658" type="x-p"/> I am become a perfect stranger in their eyes. <div eID="gen7658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7659" type="x-p"/> It may seem strange that we do not connect <reference osisRef="Job.19.12">Job 19:12</reference> with the preceding strophe or group of verses; but between <reference osisRef="Job.19.7">Job 19:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.19.21">Job 19:21</reference> there are thirty στίχοι, which, in connection with the arrangement of the rest of this speech in decastichs (accidentally coinciding remarkably with the prominence given to the number ten in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.19.3">Job 19:3</reference></hi>), seem intended to be divided into three decastichs, and can be so divided without doing violence to the connection. While in <reference osisRef="Job.19.12">Job 19:12</reference>, in connection with <reference osisRef="Job.19.11">Job 19:11</reference>, Job describes the course of the wrath, which he has to withstand as if he were an enemy of God, in Job 19:13. he refers back to the degradation complained of in Job 19:9. In <reference osisRef="Job.19.12">Job 19:12</reference> he compares himself to a besieged (perhaps on account of revolt) city. God’s גדוּדים (not: bands of marauders, as Dietr. interprets, but: troops, i.e., of regular soldiers, synon. of צבא, <reference osisRef="Job.10.17">Job 10:17</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.25.3">Job 25:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.29.25">Job 29:25</reference>, from the root גד, to unite, join, therefore prop. the assembled, a heap; vid., Fürst’s <hi type="italic">Handwörterbuch</hi>) are the bands of outwards and inward sufferings sent forth against him for a combined attack (יחד). Heaping up a way, i.e., by filling up the ramparts, is for the purpose of making the attack upon the city with battering-rams (<reference osisRef="Job.16.14">Job 16:14</reference>) and javelins, and then the storm, more effective (on this erection of offensive ramparts (<hi type="italic">approches</hi>), called elsewhere שׁפך סללה, vid., Keil’s <hi type="italic">Archäologie,</hi> §159). One result of this condition of siege in which God’s wrath has placed him is that he is avoided and despised as one smitten of God: neither love and fidelity, nor obedience and dependence, meet him from any quarter. What he has said in <reference osisRef="Job.17.6">Job 17:6</reference>, that he is become a byword and an abomination (an object to spit upon), he here describes in detail. There is no ground for understanding אחי in the wider sense of relations; brethren is meant here, as in Psa 69:9. He calls his relations קרובי, as Psa 38:12. ידעי are (in accordance with the pregnant biblical use of this word in the sense of <hi type="italic">nosse cum affectu et effectu</hi>) those who know him intimately (with objective suff. as <reference osisRef="Ps.87.4">Psa 87:4</reference>), and מידּעי, as <reference osisRef="Ps.31.12">Psa 31:12</reference>, and freq., those intimately known to him; both, therefore, so-called heart-or bosom-friends. בּיתי גּרי Jer. well translates <hi type="italic">inquilinin domus meae;</hi> they are, in distinction from those who by birth belong to the nearer and wider circle of the family, persons who are received into this circle as servants, as vassals (comp. <reference osisRef="Exod.3.22">Exo 3:22</reference>, and Arabic <hi type="italic">jâr</hi>, an associate, one sojourning in a strange country under the protection of its government, a neighbour), here espec. the domestics. The verb תּחשׁבוּני (Ges. §60) is construed with the nearest feminine subject. These people, who ought to thank him for taking them into his house, regard him as one who does not belong to it (זר); he is looked upon by them as a perfect stranger (נכרי), as an intruder from another country.
entries.72e04693c24458898a606cca30efcf8b5eb98284: <reference osisRef="Job.19.16-Job.20.16">Job 19:16-20 16</reference>  I call to my servant and he answereth not, <div eID="gen7659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7660" type="x-p"/> I am obliged to entreat him with my mouth. 17  My breath is offensive to my wife, <div eID="gen7660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7661" type="x-p"/> And my stench to my own brethren. 18  Even boys act contemptuously towards me; <div eID="gen7661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7662" type="x-p"/> If I will rise up, they speak against me. 19  All my confidential friends abhor me, <div eID="gen7662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7663" type="x-p"/> And those whom I loved have turned against me. 20  My bone cleaveth to my skin and flesh, <div eID="gen7663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7664" type="x-p"/> And I am escaped only with the skin of my teeth. <div eID="gen7664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7665" type="x-p"/> His servant, who otherwise saw every command in his eyes, and was attent upon his wink, now not only does not come at his call, but does not return him any answer. The one of the home-born slaves (vid., on <reference osisRef="Gen.14.14">Gen 14:14</reference>),<note placement="foot">The (black) slaves born within the tribe itself are in the present day, from their dependence and bravery, accounted as the stay of the tribe, and are called <hi type="italic">fadâwîje</hi>, as those who are ready to sacrifice their life for its interest. The body-slave of Job is thought of as such as יליד בית.</note> who stood in the same near connection to Job as Eliezer to Abraham, is intended here, in distinction from גרי ביתי, Job 19:15. If he, his master, now in such need of assistance, desires any service from him, he is obliged (<hi type="italic">fut</hi>. with the sense of being compelled, as e.g., <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.15.30">Job 15:30</reference></hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.17.2">Job 17:2</reference>) to entreat him with his mouth. התחנּן, to beg חן of any one for one’s self (vid., <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, p. 365), therefore to implore, <hi type="italic">supplicare;</hi> and בּמו־פּי here (as <reference osisRef="Ps.89.2">Psa 89:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.109.30">Psa 109:30</reference>) as a more significant expression of that which is loud and intentional (not as <reference osisRef="Job.16.5">Job 16:5</reference>, in contrast to that which proceeds from the heart). In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.19.17">Job 19:17</reference></hi>, רוּחי signifies neither my vexation (Hirz.) nor my spirit = I (Umbr., Hahn, with the Syr.), for רוח in the sense of angry humour (as <reference osisRef="Job.15.13">Job 15:13</reference>) does not properly suit the predicate, and Arab. <hi type="italic">rûḥy</hi> in the signification <hi type="italic">ipse</hi> may certainly be used in Arabic, where <hi type="italic">rûḥ</hi> (perhaps under the influence of the philosophical usage of the language) signifies the animal spirit-life (<hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 154), not however in Hebrew, where נפשׁי is the stereotype form in that sense. If one considers that the elephantiasis, although its proper pathological symptom consists in an enormous hypertrophy of the cellular tissue of single distinct portions of the body, still easily, if the bronchia are drawn into sympathy, or if (what is still more natural) putrefaction of the blood with a scorbutic ulcerous formation in the mouth comes on, has difficulty of breathing (<reference osisRef="Job.7.15">Job 7:15</reference>) and stinking breath as its result, as also a stinking exhalation and the discharge of a stinking fluid from the decaying limbs is connected with it (vid., the testimony of the Arabian physicians in Stickel, S. 169f.), it cannot be doubted that Jer. has lighted upon the correct thing when he transl. <hi type="italic">halitum meum exhorruit uxor mea</hi>. רוחי is intended as in <reference osisRef="Job.17.1">Job 17:1</reference>, and it is unnecessary to derive זרה from a special verb זיר, although in Arab. the notions which are united in the Hebr. זוּר .r, <hi type="italic">deflectere</hi> and <hi type="italic">abhorrere</hi> (to turn one’s self away from what is disgusting or horrible), are divided between Arab. <hi type="italic">zâr med . Wau</hi> and <hi type="italic">Arab</hi>. <hi type="italic">ḏâr med . Je</hi> (vid., Fürst’s <hi type="italic">Handwörterbuch</hi>). <div eID="gen7665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7666" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Job.19.17">Job 19:17</reference> the meaning of חנּותי is specially questionable. In <reference osisRef="Ps.77.10">Psa 77:10</reference>, חנּות is, like שׁמּות, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.3">Eze 36:3</reference>, an infinitive from חנן, formed after the manner of the <hi type="italic">Lamed He</hi> verbs. Ges. and Olsh. indeed prefer to regard these forms as plurals of substantives (חנּה, שׁמּה), but the respective passages, regarded syntactically and logically, require infinitives. As regards the accentuation, according to which וחנותי is accented by <hi type="italic">Rebia mugrasch</hi> on the <hi type="italic">ultima</hi>, this does not necessarily decide in favour of its being <hi type="italic">infin.,</hi> since in the 1 <hi type="italic">praet</hi>. סבּתי, which, according to rule, has the tone on the <hi type="italic">penultima</hi>, the <hi type="italic">ultima</hi> is also sometimes (apart from the <hi type="italic">perf. consec.</hi>) found accented (on this, vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.17.3">Psa 17:3</reference>, and Ew. §197, <hi type="italic">a</hi>), as סבּוּ, קוּמה, קוּמי, also admit of both accentuations.<note placement="foot">The <hi type="italic">ultima</hi>-accentuation of the form סבּותי is regular, is the <hi type="italic">Waw conv. praet. in fut.</hi> is added, as <reference osisRef="Exod.33.19">Exo 33:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.33.22">Exo 33:22</reference>; 2Ki 19:34; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.7">Isa 65:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.38">Eze 20:38</reference>; Mal 2:2; Psa 89:24. Besides, the <hi type="italic">penultima</hi> has the tone regularly, e.g., <reference osisRef="Josh.5.9">Jos 5:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.3">1Sa 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.22">1Sa 22:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.28">Jer 4:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.14">Psa 35:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.38.7">Psa 38:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.40.4">Job 40:4</reference>; Ecc 2:20. There are, however, exceptions, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.41">Deu 32:41</reference> (שׁנותי), <reference osisRef="Isa.44.16">Isa 44:16</reference> (חמותי), <reference osisRef="Ps.17.3">Psa 17:3</reference> (זמתי), <reference osisRef="Ps.92.11">Psa 92:11</reference> (בלתי), <reference osisRef="Ps.116.6">Psa 116:6</reference> (דלותי). Perhaps the <hi type="italic">ultima</hi>-accentuation in these exceptional instances is intended to protect the indistinct pronunciation of the consonants <hi type="italic">Beth</hi>, <hi type="italic">Waw</hi>, or even <hi type="italic">Resh</hi>, at the beginning of the following words, which might easily become blended with the final syllable תי; certainly the reason lies in the pronunciation or in the rhythm (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.116.6">Psa 116:6</reference>, and comp. the retreating of the tone in the infin. חלותי (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.11">Psa 77:11</reference>). Looking at this last exception, which has not yet been cleared up, חנותי in the present passage will always be able to be regarded on internal grounds either as infin. or as 1 praet. The <hi type="italic">ultima</hi>-accentuation makes the word at first sight appear to be <hi type="italic">infin</hi>., whereas in comparison with זרה, which is accented on the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>., and therefore as 3 <hi type="italic">praet</hi>., וחנותי seems also to be intended as <hi type="italic">praet</hi>. The accentuation, therefore, leaves the question in uncertainty.</note> <div eID="gen7666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7667" type="x-p"/> If וחנותי is <hi type="italic">infin.,</hi> the clause is a nominal clause, or a verbal one, that is to be supplemented by the <hi type="italic">v. fin.</hi> זרה; if it is first pers. <hi type="italic">praet.,</hi> we have a verbal clause. It must be determined from the matter and the connection which of these explanations, both of which are in form and syntax possible, is the correct one. <div eID="gen7667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7668" type="x-p"/> The translation, “I entreat (groan to) the sons of my body,” is not a thought that accords with the context, as would be obtained by the infin. explanation: my entreating (is offensive); this signif. (prop. to <hi type="italic">Hithp</hi>. as above) assigned to <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> by von Hofmann (<hi type="italic">Schriftbew</hi>. ii. 2, 612) is at least not to be derived from the derivative חן; it might be more easily deduced from נחנתּ, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.23">Jer 22:23</reference>, which appears to be a <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. like נחם, נאנח, from חנן, but might also be derived from ננחתּ = נאנחתּ by means of a transposition (vid., Hitz.). In the present passage one might certainly compare Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥnn</hi>, the usual word for the utterance and emotion of longing and sympathy, or also Arab. <hi type="italic">chnn , fut. i</hi> (with the infin. noun <hi type="italic">chanı̂n</hi>), which occurs in the signifn. of weeping, and transl.: my imploring, groaning, weeping, is offensive, etc. Since, however, the X. form of the Arab. <hi type="italic">chnn</hi> (<hi type="italic">istachanna</hi>) signifies to give forth an offensive smell (esp. of the stinking refuse of a well that is dried up); and besides, since the significatn. <hi type="italic">foetere</hi> is supported for the root חן (comp. צחן) by the Syriac <hi type="italic">chanı̂no</hi> (e.g., <hi type="italic">meshcho chanı̂no ,</hi> rancid oil), we may also translate: “My stinking is offensive,” etc., or: “I stink to the children of my body” (Rosenm., Ew., Hahn, Schlottm.); and this translation is not only not hazardous in a book that so abounds in derivations from the dialects, but it furnishes a thought that is as closely as possible connected with <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.19.17">Job 19:17</reference></hi>.<note placement="foot">Supplementary: Instead of <hi type="italic">istachanna</hi> (of the stinking of a well, perhaps <hi type="italic">denom</hi>. from Arab. <hi type="italic">chnn</hi>, prop. to smell like a hen-house), the verb <hi type="italic">hhannana</hi> (with Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥ</hi>) = <hi type="italic">‛affana</hi>, “to be corrupt, to have a mouldy smell,” can, with Wetzstein, be better compared with חנּותי; thence comes <hi type="italic">zêt mohhannin</hi> = <hi type="italic">mo‛affin</hi>, corrupt rancid oil, corresponding to the Syriac חנינא. Thus ambiguously to the sellers of walnuts in Damascus cry out their wares with the words: <hi type="italic">el - mohhannin maugûd</hi>, “the merciful One liveth,” i.e., I do not guarantee the quality of my wares. In like manner, not only can Arab. <hi type="italic">dâr</hi> inf. <hi type="italic">dheir</hi> (<hi type="italic">dhêr</hi>), to be offensive, be compared with זרה, but, with Wetzstein, also the very common steppe word for ”to be bad, worthless,” Arab. <hi type="italic">zrâ</hi>, whence adj. <hi type="italic">zarı̂</hi> (with nunation <hi type="italic">zarı̂jun</hi>).</note> <div eID="gen7668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7669" type="x-p"/> The further question now arises, who are meant by בטני לבני. Perhaps his children? But in the prologue these have utterly perished. Are we to suppose, with Eichhorn and Olshausen, that the poet, in the heat of discourse, forgets what he has laid down in the prologue? When we consider that this poet, within the compass of his work, - a work into which he has thrown his whole soul, - has allowed no anachronism, and no reference to anything Israelitish that is contradictory to its extra-Israelitish character, to escape him, such forgetfulness is very improbable; and when we, moreover, bear in mind that he often makes the friends refer to the destruction of Job’s children (as <reference osisRef="Job.8.4">Job 8:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.30">Job 15:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.18.16">Job 18:16</reference>), it is altogether inconceivable. Hence Schröring has proposed the following explanation: “My soul a substitution of which Hahn is also guilty is strange to my wife; my entreaty does not even penetrate to the sons of my body, it cannot reach their ear, for they are long since in Sheôl.” But he himself thinks this interpretation very hazardous and insecure; and, in fact, it is improbable that in the division, <reference osisRef="Job.19.13">Job 19:13</reference>, where Job complains of the neglect and indifference which he now experiences from those around him, בטני בני should be the only dead ones among the living, in which case it would moreover be better, after the Arabic version, to translate: “My longing is for, or: I yearn after, the children of my body.” Grandchildren (Hirz., Ew., Hlgst. Hahn) might be more readily thought of; but it is not even probable, that after having introduced the ruin of all of Job’s children, the poet would represent their children as still living, some mention of whom might then at least be expected in the epilogue. Others, again (Rosenm. Justi, Gleiss), after the precedent of the lxx (υἱοὶ παλλακίδων μου), understand the sons of concubines (slaves). Where, however, should a trace be found of the poet having conceived of his hero as a polygamist, - a hero who is even a model of chastity and continence (<reference osisRef="Job.31.1">Job 31:1</reference>)? <div eID="gen7669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7670" type="x-p"/> But must בטני בני really signify his sons or grandsons? Children certainly are frequently called, in relation to the father, בטנו פרי (e.g., <reference osisRef="Deut.7.13">Deu 7:13</reference>), and the father himself can call them בטני פרי (Mic 6:7); but בטן in this reference is not the body of the father, but the mother’s womb, whence, begotten by him, the children issue forth. Hence “son of my body” occurs only once (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.2">Pro 31:2</reference>) in the mother’s mouth. In the mouth of Job even (where the first origin of man is spoken of), בטני signifies not Job’s body, but the womb that conceived him (vid., <reference osisRef="Job.3.10">Job 3:10</reference>); and thus, therefore, it is not merely possible, but it is natural, with Stuhlm., Ges., Umbr., and Schlottm., to understand בטני בני of the sons of his mother’s womb, i.e., of her who bare him; consequently, as אמּי בני, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.9">Psa 69:9</reference>, of natural brethren (brothers and sisters, <hi type="italic">sorores uterinae</hi>), in which sense, regarding וחנותי according to the most natural influence of the tone as <hi type="italic">infin.,</hi> we transl.: “and my stinking is offensive (supply זרה) to the children of my mother’s womb.” It is also possible that the expression, as the words seem to be taken by Symmachus (υἱοὺς παιδῶν μου, my slaves’ children), and as they are taken by Kosegarten, in comparison with the Arab. <hi type="italic">btn</hi> in the signification race, subdivision (in the downward gradation, the third) of a greater tribe, may denote those who with him belong in a wider sense to one mother’s bosom, i.e., to the same clan, although the mention of בטני בני in close connection with אשׁתי is not favourable to this extension of the idea. The circle of observation is certainly widened in <reference osisRef="Job.19.18">Job 19:18</reference>, where עוילים are not Job’s grandchildren (Hahn), but the children of neighbouring families and tribes; עויל (vid., <reference osisRef="Job.16.11">Job 16:11</reference>) is a boy, and especially (perh. on account of the similarity in sound between מעוּל and עוּל) a rude, frolicsome, mischievous boy. Even such make him feel their contempt; and if with difficulty, and under the influence of pain which distorts his countenance, he attempts to raise himself (אקוּמה, lxx ὅταν ἀναστῶ, hypothetical cohortative, as <reference osisRef="Job.11.17">Job 11:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.16.6">Job 16:6</reference>), they make him the butt of their jesting talk (דּבּר בּ, as <reference osisRef="Ps.50.20">Psa 50:20</reference>).
entries.2ea1428f0f9f8c9547a8f197b80bc7a66cc20079: Job 19:21-25 21  Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, <div eID="gen7672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7673" type="x-p"/> O ye my friends, For the hand of Eloah hath touched me. 22  Wherefore do ye persecute me as God, <div eID="gen7673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7674" type="x-p"/> And are never satisfied with my flesh? 23  Oh that my words were but written, <div eID="gen7674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7675" type="x-p"/> That they were recorded in a book, 24  With an iron pen, filled in with lead, <div eID="gen7675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7676" type="x-p"/> Graven in the rock for ever! 25  And I know: my Redeemer liveth, <div eID="gen7676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7677" type="x-p"/> And as the last One will He arise from the dust. <div eID="gen7677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7678" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Job.19.21">Job 19:21</reference> Job takes up a strain we have not heard previously. His natural strength becomes more and more feeble, and his voice weaker and weaker. It is a feeling of sadness that prevails in the preceding description of suffering, and now even stamps the address to the friends with a tone of importunate entreaty which shall, if possible, affect their heart. They are indeed his friends, as the emphatic רעי אתּם affirms; impelled towards him by sympathy they are come, and at least stand by him while all other men flee from him. They are therefore to grant him favour (חנן, prop. to incline to) in the place of right; it is enough that the hand of Eloah has touched him (in connection with this, one is reminded that leprosy is called נגע, and is pre-eminently accounted as <hi type="italic">plaga divina;</hi> wherefore the suffering Messiah also bears the significant name חוּרא דבי רבּי, “the leprous one from the school of Rabbi,” in the Talmud, after <reference osisRef="Isa.53.4">Isa 53:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.8">Isa 53:8</reference>), they are not to make the divine decree heavier to him by their uncharitableness. Wherefore do ye persecute me - he asks them in <reference osisRef="Job.19.22">Job 19:22</reference> - like as God (כּמו־אל, according to Saad. and Ralbag = כמו־אלּה, which would be very tame); by which he means not merely that they add their persecution to God’s, but that they take upon themselves God’s work, that they usurp to themselves a judicial divine authority, they act towards him as if they were superhuman (vid., <reference osisRef="Isa.31.3">Isa 31:3</reference>), and therefore inhumanly, since they, who are but his equals, look down upon him from an assumed and false elevation. The other half of the question: wherefore are ye not full of my flesh (<hi type="italic">de ma chair,</hi> with מן, as <reference osisRef="Job.31.31">Job 31:31</reference>), but still continue to devour it? is founded upon a common Semitic figurative expression, with which may be compared our Germ. expression, “to gnaw with the tooth of slander” comp. Engl. “backbiting”. In Chaldee, אכל קרצוהי די, to eat the pieces of (any one), is equivalent to, to slander him; in Syriac, <hi type="italic">ochelqarsso</hi> is the name of Satan, like διάβολος. The Arabic here, as almost everywhere in the book of Job, presents a still closer parallel; for Arab. <hi type="italic">'kl lḥm</hi> signifies to eat any one’s flesh, then (different from אכל בשׂר, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.2">Psa 27:2</reference>) equivalent to, to slander,<note placement="foot">Vid., Schultens’ <hi type="italic">ad Prov. Meidanii</hi>, p. 7 (where “to eat his own flesh,” equivalent to “himself,” without allowing others to do it, signifies to censure his kinsmen), and comp. the phrase Arab. <hi type="italic">aclu - l - a‛râdhi</hi> in the signification <hi type="italic">arrodere existimationem hominum</hi> in Makkari, i. 541, 13.</note> since an evil report is conceived of as a wild beast, which delights in tearing a neighbour to pieces, as the friends do not refrain from doing, since, from the love of their assumption that his suffering must be the retributive punishment of heinous sins, they lay sins to his charge of which he is not conscious, and which he never committed. Against these uncharitable and groundless accusations he wishes (<reference osisRef="Job.19.23">Job 19:23</reference>) that the testimony of his innocence, to which they will not listen, might be recorded in a book for posterity, or because a book may easily perish, graven in a rock (therefore not on leaden plates) with an iron style, and the addition of lead, with which to fill up the engraved letters, and render them still more imperishable. In connection with the remarkable fidelity with which the poet throws himself back into the pre-Israelitish patriarchal time of his hero, it is of no small importance that he ascribes to him an acquaintance not only with monumental writing, but also with book and documentary writing (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.31.35">Job 31:35</reference>). <div eID="gen7678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7679" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">fut.,</hi> which also elsewhere (<reference osisRef="Job.6.8">Job 6:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.13.5">Job 13:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.14.13">Job 14:13</reference>, once the <hi type="italic">praet.,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.23.3">Job 23:3</reference>, <hi type="italic">noverim</hi>) follows מי־יתּן, <hi type="italic">quis dabat</hi> = <hi type="italic">utinam</hi>, has <hi type="italic">Waw consec.</hi> here (as <reference osisRef="Deut.5.26">Deu 5:26</reference> the <hi type="italic">praet.</hi>); the arrangement of the words is extremely elegant, בּסּפר stands <hi type="italic">per hyperbaton</hi> emphatically prominent. כּתב and חקק (whence <hi type="italic">fut. Hoph.</hi> יחקוּ with <hi type="italic">Dag. implicitum</hi> in the ח, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.4.20">Job 4:20</reference>, and the <hi type="italic">Dag.</hi> of the ק omitted, for יוּחקּוּ, according to Ges. §67, rem. 8) interchange also elsewhere, Isa 30:8. ספר, according to its etymon, is a book formed of the skin of an animal, as Arab. <hi type="italic">sufre</hi>, the leathern table-mat spread on the ground instead of a table. It is as unnecessary to read לעד (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.16.8">Job 16:8</reference>, lxx, εἰς μαρτύριον) instead of לעד here, as in Isa 30:8. He wishes that his own declaration, in opposition to his accusers, may be inscribed as on a monument, that it may be immortalized,<note placement="foot">לעד is differently interpreted by Jerome: evermore hewn in the rock; for so it seems his <hi type="italic">vel certe</hi> (instead of which <hi type="italic">celte</hi> is also read, which is an old northern name for a chisel) <hi type="italic">sculpantur in siliece</hi> must be explained.</note> in order that posterity may behold it, and, it is to be hoped, judge him more justly than his contemporaries. He wishes this, and is certain that his wish is not vain. His testimony to his innocence will not descend to posterity without being justified to it by God, the living God. <div eID="gen7679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7680" type="x-p"/> Thus is ואני ידעתּי connected with what precedes. yd`ty is followed, as in <reference osisRef="Job.30.23">Job 30:23</reference>, Ps. 9:21, by the <hi type="italic">oratio directa. </hi> The monosyllable tone-word חי (on account of which go'aliy has the accent drawn back to the <hi type="italic">penult.</hi>) is 3 <hi type="italic">praet.:</hi> I know: my redeemer liveth; in connection with this we recall the name of God, חי העולם, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.7">Dan 12:7</reference>, after which the Jewish oath <hi type="italic">per Anchialum</hi> in Martial is to be explained. גּאל might (with Umbr. and others), in comparison with <reference osisRef="Job.16.18">Job 16:18</reference>, as Num 35:12, be equivalent to גּאל הדּם: he who will redeem, demand back, avenge the shedding of his blood and maintain his honour as of blood that has been innocently shed; in general, however, g'l signifies to procure compensation for the down-trodden and unjustly oppressed, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.11">Pro 23:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.58">Lam 3:58</reference>; Psa 119:154. This Rescuer of his honour lives and will rise up as the last One, as one who holds out over everything, and therefore as one who will speak the final decisive word. To אחרון have been given the significations Afterman in the sense of <hi type="italic">vindex</hi> (Hirz., Ewald), or Rearman in the sense of a second [<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. in a duel,] (Hahn), but contrary to the usage of the language: the word signifies <hi type="italic">postremus, novissimus,</hi> and is to be understood according to <reference osisRef="Isa.44.6">Isa 44:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.12">Isa 48:12</reference>, comp. Job 41:4. But what is the meaning of על־עפר? Is it: upon the dust of the earth, having descended from heaven? The words may, according to <reference osisRef="Job.41.25">Job 41:25</reference> [Hebr., Engl. Job 41:33], be understood thus (without the accompanying notion, formerly supposed by Umbreit, of <hi type="italic">pulvis</hi> or <hi type="italic">arena</hi> = <hi type="italic">palaestra</hi>, which is Classic, not Hebraic); but looking to the process of destruction going on in his body, which has been previously the subject of his words, and is so further on, it is far more probable that על־עפר is to be interpreted according to <reference osisRef="Job.17.16">Job 17:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.20.11">Job 20:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.26">Job 21:26</reference>; Psa 30:10. Moreover, an Arab would think of nothing else but the dust of the grave if he read Arab. <hi type="italic">‛alâ turâbin</hi>in this connection.<note placement="foot">In Arabic <hi type="italic">‛fr</hi> belongs only to the ancient language (whence <hi type="italic">‛afarahu</hi>, he has cast him into the dust, placed him upon the sand, inf. <hi type="italic">‛afr</hi>); Arab. <hi type="italic">gbâr</hi> (whence the <hi type="italic">Ghobar</hi>, a peculiar secret-writing, has its name) signifies the dry, flying dust; Arab. <hi type="italic">trâb</hi>, however, is dust in gen., and particularly the dust of the grave, as e.g., in the forcible proverb: nothing but the <hi type="italic">turâb</hi> fills the eyes of man. So common is this signification, that a tomb is therefore called <hi type="italic">turbe</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen7680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7681" type="x-p"/> Besides, it is unnecessary to connect קום על, as perhaps <reference osisRef="2Chr.21.4">2Ch 21:4</reference>, and the Arab. <hi type="italic">qâm ‛alâ</hi> (to stand by, help): על־עפר is first of all nothing more than a defining of locality. To affirm that if it refer to Job it ought to be עפרי, is unfounded. Upon the dust in which he is now soon to be laid, into which he is now soon to be changed, will He, the Rescuer of his honour, arise (קוּם, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.19.15">Deu 19:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.27.12">Psa 27:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.11">Psa 35:11</reference>, of the rising up of a witness, and as e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.12.6">Psa 12:6</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.94.16">Psa 94:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.10">Isa 33:10</reference>, of the rising up and interposing of a rescuer and help) and set His divine seal to Job’s own testimony thus made permanent in the monumental inscription. Oetinger’s interpretation is substantially the same: “I know that He will at last come, place himself over the dust in which I have mouldered away, pronounce my cause just, and place upon me the crown of victory.” <div eID="gen7681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7682" type="x-p"/> A somewhat different connection of the thought is obtained, if ואני is taken not progressively, but adversatively: “Yet I know,” etc. The thought is then, that his testimony of his innocence need not at all be inscribed in the rock; on the contrary, God, the ever living One, will verify it. It is difficult to decide between them; still the progressive rendering seems to be preferable, because the human vindication after death, which is the object of the wish expressed in <reference osisRef="Job.19.23">Job 19:23</reference>, is still not essentially different from the divine vindication hoped for in <reference osisRef="Job.19.25">Job 19:25</reference>, which must not be regarded as an antithesis, but rather as a perfecting of the other designed for posterity. <reference osisRef="Job.19.25">Job 19:25</reference> is, however, certainly a higher hope, to which the wish in Job 19:23. forms the stepping-stone. God himself will avenge Job’s blood, i.e., against his accusers, who say that it is the blood of one who is guilty; over the dust of the departed He will arise, and by His majestic testimony put to silence those who regard this dust of decay as the dust of a sinner, who has received the reward of his deeds. <div eID="gen7682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7683" type="x-p"/> But is it perhaps this his hope of God’s vindication, expressed in <reference osisRef="Job.19.25">Job 19:25</reference>, which (as Schlottmann and Hahn,<note placement="foot">Hahn, after having in his pamphlet, <hi type="italic">de spe immortalitatis sub V.T. gradatim exculta</hi>, 1845, understood Job’s confession distinctly of a future beholding in this world, goes further in his <hi type="italic">Commentary</hi>, and entirely deprives this confession of the character of hope, and takes all as an expression of what is present. We withhold our further assent.</note> though in other respects giving very different interpretations, think) is, according to Job’s wish, to be permanently inscribed on the monument, in order to testify to posterity with what a stedfast and undismayed conviction he had died? The high-toned <hi type="italic">introitus</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.19.23">Job 19:23</reference>, would be worthy of the important inscription it introduces. But (1) it is improbable that the inscription would begin with ואני, consequently with <hi type="italic">Waw</hi>, - a difficulty which is not removed by the translation, “Yea, I know,” but only covered up; the appeal to <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Psa 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.14">Isa 3:14</reference>, is inadmissible, since there the divine utterance, which begins with <hi type="italic">Waw, per aposiopesin</hi> continues a suppressed clause; כי אני would be more admissible, but that which is to be written down does not even begin with כי in either <reference osisRef="Hab.2.3">Hab 2:3</reference> or Jer 30:3. (2.)
